findings.quote: In recent external audits completed across authorities in Berkshire, it was noted that there is no record of full Cabinet having agreed the full disregard following the creation of Unitary authorities.

findings.headline: Government SEND deficit support grant covers only 90%; council responsible for remaining 10% from depleted reserves.
findings.detail: Government funding covers 90% of historic SEND deficits accrued to March 2026 for councils with approved reform plans. Slough funds the remaining 10% from own resources. The auditor will evaluate grant recognition and include in VFM assessment.
findings.matters: The council's share of a historic SEND deficit represents a significant call on already-depleted reserves and signals ongoing service delivery challenges in a high-cost area.
findings.figures: Council responsible for 10% of historical SEND deficit (total size not stated)
findings.quote: The Government has announced funding to cover 90% of historic deficits accrued up to March 2026 for Councils that secure approval of a local SEND reform plan and the Council would be responsible for meeting the remaining 10% of this deficit.

findings.headline: Historical group consolidation errors including over-accrual of subsidiary profits remain uncorrected; 2025/26 is first group audit since 2018/19.
findings.detail: The 2018/19 audit identified material errors: over-accrual of subsidiary profits and misclassification of subsidiary loans as equity. No group audit completed since 2018/19 (seven-year gap). Council control weaknesses cascade to subsidiaries. Group consolidation flagged as significant risk for 2025/26.
findings.matters: Errors in group consolidation materially misstate the council's consolidated financial position. A seven-year audit gap means prior errors may remain uncorrected and subsidiary financial exposure is unknown.
findings.figures: 7-year gap in group audits (2018/19 to 2025/26); material prior errors unresolved
findings.quote: Material issues identified included the over-accrual of anticipated profits related to the Council's interest in subsidiaries and the improper accounting of a loan granted to a subsidiary as an equity investment instead of a soft loan.

findings.headline: IFRS 16 lease accounting standard mandated from April 2024 has not been implemented; no audit work completed in 2024/25 due to late financial statement delivery.
findings.detail: IFRS 16 became mandatory for local government from 1 April 2024. The council has not implemented it; no audit work was completed in 2024/25 due to delayed financial statement delivery. The auditor notes the council has 'previously faced challenges producing up to date financial statements' and flags IFRS16 implementation as an 'other risk'.
findings.matters: Non-implementation of a mandatory accounting standard suggests the council's financial reporting infrastructure cannot keep pace with regulatory requirements, indicating fundamental capacity issues in financial management.
findings.figures: Mandatory from 1 April 2024 (nearly 2 years overdue for implementation)
findings.quote: Due to delays in receiving the financial statements, no work on IFRS16 implementation as part of the 2024/25 financial statements audit, including PFI. We have therefore continued to identify an 'other risk' in relation to the identification and classification of leases under IFRS 16.

findings.headline: Audit fee increased 53% to £560,547 in 2025-26 from £366,565, reflecting additional complexity; excludes separate charges for disclaimed years
findings.detail: The audit fee rose from £366,565 (2024/25) to £560,547 (2025/26)—a 53% increase including £10,000 each for valuations and IFRS16 work. The base increase reflects additional complexity. Critically, this does not include separate charges for rebuilding assurance over disclaimed years. Further increases possible if accounts quality is poor.
findings.matters: Rapidly escalating audit costs indicate increasingly troubled accounts and controls. Ongoing escalation is unsustainable and may eventually render accounts unauditable, preventing compliance with statutory financial reporting.
findings.quote: Our proposed fee for the audit is £560,547 (PY: £366,565) for the Council, subject to the Council delivering a good set of financial statements and working papers, no significant changes in scope to the Audit, management being responsive to audit requests and providing sufficient appropriate audit evidence when requested.

findings.headline: Statutory recommendation requiring urgent action on low levels of unearmarked and earmarked revenue reserves
findings.detail: The Value for Money assessment retains a statutory recommendation (strongest audit criticism) requiring urgent action on reserve depletion. The auditor notes continuing concern about the council's medium-term financial viability and ability to develop sustainability plans.
findings.matters: Depleted reserves provide minimal buffer for expenditure shocks or service disruptions, increasing financial fragility and risk to debt sustainability and service continuity.
findings.figures: Specific reserve levels not quantified (characterised as 'low')
findings.quote: The Council should take urgent action to address its low levels of unearmarked and earmarked revenue reserves (statutory recommendation)

findings.headline: Minimum Revenue Provision charge was understated for multiple years, resulting in material misstatement of reserve balances.
findings.detail: The 2018/19 audit identified that MRP (the statutory debt repayment provision) had been understated for multiple years, causing material misstatement of both usable and unusable reserves. The calculation remains high-risk due to fixed asset register deficiencies and complexity from capitalisation directions.
findings.matters: MRP understatement means insufficient funds set aside for debt repayment, overstating available reserves and understating future financial obligations—misrepresenting the true financial position.
findings.figures: Multiple years understated (specific amounts not quantified)
findings.quote: The last completed audit for (2018/19) identified that the Council's Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) charge had been understated for multiple years, resulting in a material misstatement of the related usable and unusable reserve balances.

findings.headline: Material unreconciled cash balances exceeding £20 million from the 2018/19 audit remain unresolved.
findings.detail: The 2018/19 audit identified significant cash reconciliation deficiencies when ledger systems changed but reconciliation processes were not properly updated. The council's records showed over £20 million in unmatched transactions. Further investigations by PwC were ongoing but results unreported. This remains flagged as a significant risk for 2025/26.
findings.matters: Unreconciled cash of this magnitude indicates missing transactions, recording errors, or potential fraud. It prevents accurate assessment of liquidity and suggests inadequate controls over cash handling.
findings.figures: Over £20 million in unmatched transactions
findings.quote: The Council's records indicated over £20 million in unmatched transactions, and further investigations were being conducted by PwC. The results of this work may have an impact on the financial statements, including amounts within the accounts receivable and the Comprehensive Income and Expenditure accounts.

findings.headline: Slough has applied for Exceptional Financial Support from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government.
findings.detail: The council has applied for EFS funding, the government's support programme for authorities in serious financial difficulty. The auditor's plan includes procedures to confirm the Capitalisation Direction has been formally issued by the Secretary of State, indicating approval is expected and will be material to the accounts.
findings.matters: An EFS application signals severe financial distress and indicates the council's own resources are insufficient to cover planned spending—critical for assessing debt sustainability and ability to service borrowing.
findings.figures: Application made (specific amount not disclosed)
findings.quote: The Council has applied for EFS from the Ministry of Housing, Communities, and Local Government (MHCLG)

findings.headline: Auditor has issued disclaimer of opinion for 2024/25 and the preceding six years, leaving the council's financial position unaudited since 2017/18.
findings.detail: The auditor issued a disclaimer of opinion on the 2024/25 accounts due to the backstop deadline. This follows disclaimed opinions for the preceding six years. As a result, for 2025/26 the auditor will have no assurance over opening balances and cannot assure the closing reserves balance. The audit strategy focuses on in-year transactions rather than rebuilding assurance over prior balances.
findings.matters: An unaudited financial position makes it impossible for external parties to rely on the accounts to assess the council's true financial health, reserves, or debt position—a fundamental requirement for lending decisions.
findings.figures: 7 consecutive years of disclaimed opinions (2017/18 through 2024/25)
findings.quote: In the audit report for the year ended 31 March 2025, a disclaimer of opinion was issued due to the backstop. Disclaimer opinions were also issued for the preceding 6 years. As a result, we anticipate that for 2025/26: we will have no assurance over the opening balances for 2025/26; and no assurance over the closing reserves balance, due to the uncertainty over their opening amount.

findings.headline: General Fund Asset Disposal Programme delays and market volatility moved risk from yellow to amber
findings.detail: CR10 (Failure of General Fund Asset Disposal Programme) escalated from yellow to amber due to market volatility and delays to completion. Asset sales are often assumed in council financial plans as revenue contributions from capital receipts, so delays reduce forecast income certainty.
findings.matters: Asset disposal delays suggest planned revenue contributions from capital receipts may not materialise on schedule, affecting cash-based budget forecasting.
findings.figures: Risk rating increased from yellow to amber; drivers cited are market volatility and completion delays
findings.quote: CR10: Failure of General Fund Asset Disposal Programme – The overall rating increased from yellow to amber, driven by SR10.01 due to market volatility and delays to completion.

findings.headline: Loss of Health and Safety Manager caused risk rating to escalate from yellow to amber
findings.detail: CR06 (Health and Safety: Failure to Meet Statutory Obligations) increased from yellow to amber following the loss of the Health and Safety Manager. Although this has been mitigated by appointment of external consultants, the incident demonstrates dependency on specific key individuals for governance compliance.
findings.matters: Loss of a single manager causing an immediate risk increase shows shallow bench strength and potential key person dependencies in critical governance roles.
findings.figures: Risk rating increased from yellow to amber; subsequently mitigated by external consultant appointment
findings.quote: CR06: Health and Safety – Failure to Meet Statutory Obligations – The overall rating increased from yellow to amber, driven by SR06.04 following the loss of the Health and Safety Manager. This has since been mitigated through the appointment of external consultants.

findings.headline: Council is operating under statutory direction with government commissioners appointed
findings.detail: The council is under statutory direction from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) with commissioners formally appointed. A new statutory direction was issued in November 2024 with specific actions linked to management of risk, including a required improvement and recovery plan, following a finding that the council failed to meet its best value duty.
findings.matters: Statutory direction with external commissioners indicates past governance failure and ongoing central government intervention, a significant governance and credit risk signal.
findings.figures: Statutory direction issued November 2024; commissioners appointed; improvement and recovery plan mandated
findings.quote: This has resulted in the Council being under statutory direction of the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) and having appointed commissioners under a formal direction. A new statutory direction was issued in November 2024

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation demand pressure persists despite modestly improved risk score
findings.detail: CR04 (Failure to Provide Safe Temporary Accommodation within Budget) remains red-rated but with an improved score (reduced from 25 to 23). However, the report emphasises that the primary driver of risk is 'still the availability of suitable accommodation to meet demand, as opposed to just the cost'. This indicates demand-side pressures will persist.
findings.matters: Persistent temporary accommodation pressure driven by availability rather than cost alone suggests a structural homelessness/housing issue that will continue to consume council resources.
findings.figures: Risk score reduced from 25 to 23 but remains red; primary driver is accommodation availability not cost
findings.quote: Although the overall score reduced the primary driver of the risk is still the availability of suitable accommodation to meet demand, as opposed to just the cost of accommodation.

findings.headline: Two new red-rated corporate risks were added to the register this quarter
findings.detail: CR11 (Failure to Deliver Transformation Portfolio) and CR15 (Failure of Governance, Controls and Assurance) were approved by the Risk Management Board and Corporate Leadership Team this quarter as new red risks. These additions increased the total corporate risks from 13 to 15 and suggest issues that were previously untracked at corporate level are now escalated.
findings.matters: New red-rated risks appearing in corporate governance reporting, particularly one on governance and assurance itself, suggest control framework gaps are being identified.
findings.figures: Two new red risks added; total corporate risks increased from 13 to 15
findings.quote: two new corporate risks have now been approved by the Risk Management Board and the Corporate Leadership Team have now gone live this quarter

findings.headline: Financial sustainability risk CR09 remains red-rated, driven by failure to achieve balanced budget and Medium-Term Financial Strategy
findings.detail: CR09 (Failure to achieve financial sustainability and a balanced MTFS) remains red-rated with a stable outlook. The risk is specifically driven by the sub-risk of failure to achieve a balanced budget and Medium-Term Financial Strategy. This reflects a structural inability to close the budget gap through the planned medium term.
findings.matters: A persistent red-rated financial sustainability risk signals that the council lacks a credible medium-term plan to balance the budget, a fundamental concern for any lender.
findings.figures: Remains in red category; no score change reported this quarter
findings.quote: CR09: (Failure to achieve financial sustainability and a balanced MTFS) – the risk remains red and is reported as being stable. It is still driven by the sub-risk for the failure to achieve a balanced budget and Medium-Term Financial Strategy (MTFS).

findings.headline: Adult Social Care is forecasting a £4.7m overspend as of end P10 2026/27
findings.detail: The ASC directorate is forecasting a £4.7m overspend at end of P10 2026/27, comprising provider uplifts and new demand from new service users and increased need. This is despite the risk score having improved from red to amber (20 to 17), as the budget was re-baselined. The forecast indicates actual spend is significantly exceeding the revised budget plan.
findings.matters: A £4.7m forecast overspend in a service that is normally the largest discretionary spend indicates demand-driven cost escalation that budget planning is not containing.
findings.figures: £4.7m overspend forecast at end of P10 2026/27 against revised budget
findings.quote: at end of P10 there is a forecast of £4.7m overspend which includes provider uplifts and new demand related to new people/increase in need

findings.headline: Children's Social Care ended with £1,734,000 deficit and is requesting in-year funding from the council
findings.detail: Slough Children's First (SCF) ended 2026/7 with a £1.7m deficit and has submitted an in-year request to cover it. Costs remain high in 2026/7 with emerging demand pressures from ongoing high-cost complex cases, and the risk remains red with a stable outlook. If not funded, the deficit would need to come from council reserves.
findings.matters: A £1.7m+ unplanned in-year call on council reserves signals structural demand problems in a service that is a significant contingent liability for any borrower.
findings.figures: £1,734,000 deficit in 2026/7; additional emergency funding request submitted
findings.quote: SCF ended 2026/7 with a deficit of £1,734,000 and has submitted an in-year request to cover this. Costs remain high in 2026/7 and a request has been made to the Council to fund these emerging demand pressures.

findings.headline: Another disclaimed opinion expected for 2025/26 despite one-year rebuild effort
findings.detail: Even with focused audit work on 2025/26 in-year transactions and closing balances, the auditor does not expect to support an unmodified opinion on the 2025/26 financial statements. A disclaimer is anticipated.
findings.matters: Despite a dedicated rebuild year with auditor focus on in-year transactions, the council is still unable to provide audit assurance, confirming the depth of the systemic issues.
findings.figures: Sign-off target: 30 November 2026; opinion: disclaimed
findings.quote: Following disclaimed audit reports for the years 2018/19 to 2024/25, we do not expect to be able to support an unmodified opinion on the 2025/26 financial statements

findings.headline: Reserves assurance cannot be regained through audit procedures alone
findings.detail: The auditor identifies that reserves are complex and have had no audit assurance for five years. Due to weak audit trails, high error rates, and other control weaknesses, the auditor explicitly states it may not be possible to regain assurance through audit procedures alone.
findings.matters: Reserves are a critical indicator of financial position; the auditor's statement that assurance may not be achievable indicates a material risk to the financial statements.
findings.figures: Five years without audit assurance over reserves (through 2024/25); assurance not expected until 2030/31
findings.quote: The Authority is required to present its reserves in a prescribed manner, with balances arising from statutory requirements and ringfences, which are complex and have not been subject to audit assurance for five years... These factors significantly increase the risk of material misstatement in reserves, and it may not be possible to regain assurance through audit procedures alone

findings.headline: Section 114 notice issued in July 2021 indicating inability to balance budget
findings.detail: The council issued a Section 114 notice in July 2021, which formally indicates the council's chief financial officer believed the council could not balance its budget and required intervention.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice signals formal financial distress and triggers government intervention; it is a material governance failure.
findings.figures: Section 114 notice: July 2021
findings.quote: the issuance of a Section 114 notice in July 2021

findings.headline: Council has not published draft financial statements in accordance with statutory deadlines in previous years, impeding audit procedures
findings.detail: Slough has not published its draft financial statements in accordance with statutory deadlines in previous years. The auditor explicitly states this has impeded their ability to undertake sufficient audit procedures.
findings.matters: Inability to meet statutory publication deadlines is a governance failure and directly constrains the auditor's ability to complete the audit on time.
findings.figures: Multiple years of missed statutory publication deadlines
findings.quote: The Authority's draft financial statements have not been published in accordance with the statutory deadline in previous years. Our tenure as auditors commenced in 2018/19. In that first year of audit, we identified a high volume of misstatements and control deficiencies which culminated in a significant number of prior period adjustments and resulted in the 2018/19 audit opinion being fully disclaimed. Since then, the Authority has struggled to deliver draft financial statements in line with the statutory publication deadlines which has impeded our ability to undertake sufficient and appropriate audit procedures to support an audit opinion

findings.headline: High turnover in finance team with risk of institutional knowledge gaps
findings.detail: The finance team experienced high turnover during the years of disclaimed opinions. While resource position is more stable for 2025/26, the auditor identifies a risk that there is a lack of understanding of prior year accounting transactions.
findings.matters: Finance team capacity and continuity directly affects ability to rebuild audit assurance and maintain financial control; knowledge gaps increase misstatement risk.
findings.figures: High turnover noted for entire period 2018/19–2024/25 (seven years)
findings.quote: The Authority's finance team has experienced a high degree of turnover during the period for which disclaimed audit opinions have been issued. While the overall resource position is more stable for 2025/26, there remains a risk that there is a lack of understanding of prior year accounting transactions

findings.headline: Audit identified control weaknesses across data quality, payroll reporting, audit evidence, accounts production and incomplete IFRS 16 application
findings.detail: The auditor identified audit limitations and control weaknesses including poor data quality, payroll reporting issues, incomplete audit evidence, delays in accounts production, and material financial reporting deficiencies such as errors and incomplete application of IFRS 16. The auditor notes the overall control environment and audit readiness are still weak.
findings.matters: Weak controls increase the risk of material misstatement, fraud, and financial losses; rebuilding these will take years.
findings.figures: Control weaknesses across: data quality, payroll, audit evidence, accounts production, IFRS 16 compliance, audit trails, error rates in samples, schools' cash, lease accounting, debtors, creditors
findings.quote: Audit limitations and control weaknesses remain, including poor data quality, payroll reporting issues, incomplete audit evidence, and delays in accounts production, alongside material financial reporting deficiencies such as errors and incomplete application of IFRS 16

findings.headline: Six-year recovery plan; clean opinion not expected until 2030/31
findings.detail: The auditor's trajectory shows disclaimed opinions continuing through 2028/29, transition to qualified opinion in 2029/30, and only an unmodified (clean) opinion anticipated in 2030/31. This is an exceptionally extended recovery timeline reflecting the depth of the problems.
findings.matters: Lenders require auditable financial statements; a six-year wait for a clean opinion is extraordinary and indicates very serious underlying issues.
findings.figures: 2025/26–2028/29: Disclaimed; 2029/30: Qualified; 2030/31: Unmodified (clean)
findings.quote: 2030/31: Unqualified: Unmodified opinion anticipated, subject to satisfactory completion of the build-back work programme and absence of any new significant issues

findings.headline: Formally assessed as Category D with major systemic problems
findings.detail: Under MHCLG's capacity assessment framework, Slough is provisionally assessed as Category D, indicating the council is not capable of achieving an ISA-compliant audit approach by 2027/28 due to major systemic problems. This is the lowest assessment category.
findings.matters: This is MHCLG's formal finding that Slough has major systemic problems; the assessment is shared with government as part of reviewing local government capacity.
findings.figures: Category D assessment; target year for ISA compliance: 2027/28 (not achievable under current trajectory)
findings.quote: we have provisionally assessed this audit as Category D

findings.headline: Seven consecutive years of disclaimed audit opinions with no clean opinion since 2017/18
findings.detail: Slough has received disclaimer of opinion for every year from 2018/19 through 2024/25, meaning the council has no audit assurance over its financial statements for seven years. The auditor explicitly states the council has not received a clean audit opinion since 2017/18.
findings.matters: No audit assurance for seven years is unprecedented and signals fundamental inability to produce auditable financial statements or maintain adequate controls.
findings.quote: The Council has not had a clean audit opinion since 2017/18

findings.headline: New governance theme created following Regulator of Social Housing inspection of council housing services
findings.detail: Housing services governance appears for the first time as a separate theme because 'This is a new governance theme and reflects the outcome of the Regulator of Social Housing inspection.' This means the regulator has identified issues requiring formal governance response.
findings.matters: A new regulatory finding suggests either deteriorating control or a newly discovered problem. Housing regulator intervention can require remediation spending or constraints on housing business decisions.
findings.figures: 2 housing governance actions, 3 property asset actions
findings.quote: This is a new governance theme and reflects the outcome of the Regulator of Social Housing inspection. The actions focus on strategic framework and annual reporting on complaints.

findings.headline: Children's services regulatory issues, carried over from prior year inspections
findings.detail: Actions on children's services 'are carried over from the previous year and align to more recent inspections highlighting regulatory issues with service delivery.' This suggests prior inspection findings have not been resolved, and recent inspections have confirmed ongoing problems.
findings.matters: Regulatory failure in children's services can trigger intervention, require additional costly remediation, or result in demand-led spending increases. Unresolved prior-year issues indicate weak execution capability.
findings.figures: 3 children's services governance actions carried over
findings.quote: These actions are carried over from the previous year and align to more recent inspections highlighting regulatory issues with service delivery.

findings.headline: Commissioners note action plan is overloaded and risks diluting focus from critical priorities
findings.detail: The commissioners' review states: 'with the high volume of actions outlined, the plan risks being unmanageable and diluting focus on the most critical risks. The committee will need to streamline, prioritise, and consolidate the plan to focus on the significant and material weaknesses.' This signals concern that the council is trying to fix too much at once.
findings.matters: An overloaded action plan is often a sign of uncontrolled problems that no one has prioritised. It suggests the council may fail to deliver on the highest-risk items.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: with the high volume of actions outlined, the plan risks being unmanageable and diluting focus on the most critical risks. The committee will need to streamline, prioritise, and consolidate the plan to focus on the significant and material weaknesses.

findings.headline: Risk management, asset management, and procurement controls require further strengthening
findings.detail: The assessment identifies material gaps: 'Risk culture, business continuity testing, asset management, procurement and contract management, counter fraud and controlled entity oversight require further strengthening.' These are core financial controls.
findings.matters: Weak procurement and contract management directly affects the council's ability to get value for money in major commitments. Weak asset management can mask asset deterioration or impairment. Weak counter-fraud controls suggest potential loss exposure.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Risk culture, business continuity testing, asset management, procurement and contract management, counter fraud and controlled entity oversight require further strengthening.

findings.headline: High staff turnover and unclear delegations affecting organisational capacity and resilience
findings.detail: Capacity and capability are identified as challenged by 'High turnover, unclear internal delegations, need for stronger member and officer governance training, and workforce capacity issues continue to affect resilience.' High turnover typically signals either instability in leadership or difficulty retaining experienced financial staff.
findings.matters: Finance and governance require continuity of knowledge and relationships. High turnover in finance or audit functions increases risk of errors, missed deadlines, and loss of institutional memory around complex financial arrangements.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: High turnover, unclear internal delegations, need for stronger member and officer governance training, and workforce capacity issues continue to affect resilience.

findings.headline: Historic audit recommendations remain open, unresolved from prior years
findings.detail: The assessment explicitly states that 'Historic audit recommendations remain open,' without specifying how many or which ones. This indicates prior identified control weaknesses have not been remediated.
findings.matters: Open audit recommendations are a red flag that the council is either unable or unwilling to address identified control failures. This undermines confidence in the reliability of financial statements and internal controls.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Historic audit recommendations remain open, improvement plans are not always clearly resourced, complaints ownership needs strengthening and reports can be overly technical.

findings.headline: Multiple financial governance actions carried over from prior year, indicating slow progress on finance improvement plans
findings.detail: The action plan notes that among six financial governance actions, 'Many of these actions are carried over from the previous year and are part of detailed finance improvement plans.' This suggests prior-year finance governance issues remain unresolved.
findings.matters: Repeated failure to complete planned governance improvements indicates either lack of capacity or lack of prioritisation. Either signals difficulty delivering promised financial control improvements.
findings.figures: 6 financial governance actions, many carried over
findings.quote: Many of these actions are carried over from the previous year and are part of detailed finance improvement plans. Progress against these have been reported separately to the committee.

findings.headline: Budget monitoring and service planning not consistently aligned across the organisation
findings.detail: The assessment finds that 'Service planning, budget monitoring, self-assessment and performance management are not yet consistently aligned across the organisation.' This fragmentation means financial reporting may not reflect actual performance or emerging pressures across services.
findings.matters: Lenders and finance directors rely on accurate, timely budget monitoring to identify problems early. Misalignment suggests variance reporting is unreliable.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Service planning, budget monitoring, self-assessment and performance management are not yet consistently aligned across the organisation.

findings.headline: Financial sustainability and service strategies remain underdeveloped, with gaps in business cases and options appraisal
findings.detail: The council identifies that 'Corporate vision, service strategies and financial sustainability remain underdeveloped, with gaps in business cases, options appraisal and fair access arrangements in key services.' This suggests the council lacks a clear basis for major spending and investment decisions.
findings.matters: Weak financial planning and business case discipline suggests the council may be unable to reliably evaluate savings opportunities, and risk decisions are made without proper justification.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Corporate vision, service strategies and financial sustainability remain underdeveloped, with gaps in business cases, options appraisal and fair access arrangements in key services.

findings.headline: Council's governance assessment finds systems not yet mature enough to identify compliance issues
findings.detail: The council's own assessment states that despite improvements, governance is not mature enough across the organisation to be fit for purpose. Critically, compliance remains an issue and 'the systems are not yet mature enough to easily identify these compliance issues.' This means the council may not know when it is breaching governance standards or financial controls.
findings.matters: A lender needs assurance that a council can identify and manage compliance failures. If systems cannot reliably surface problems, there is elevated risk of hidden financial or legal exposure.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: governance is not yet mature enough across the organisation to assess it as fit for purpose. The written systems are in general appropriate, with some limited exceptions, however compliance remains an issue and the systems are not yet mature enough to easily identify these compliance issues.

findings.headline: Asset disposal programme carries £0.3m+ annual risk; market volatility could reduce proceeds
findings.detail: The council is relying on property sales to help balance its budget. The register identifies property market volatility as creating risk. Prudent assumptions have already been applied to the disposal target, and the risk register quantifies further prudence of £0.3m+ annually.
findings.matters: Asset sales are a one-off source of funding that cannot be repeated indefinitely. Market downturn would eliminate a key part of the financial recovery plan.
findings.quote: The number and value of assets that could potentially be sold is a key element in setting the financial target for the programme.

findings.headline: General inflation across all contracts is running ahead of 2% MTFS assumption; OBR forecasts are higher
findings.detail: The council notes that 'Inflation in 2025/26 and across the MTFS is higher than projections built into the budget' and that the October 2024 OBR forecast exceeds MTFS assumptions. Each additional 1% of inflation costs approximately £0.750m across all three years.
findings.matters: This is a broad-based cost pressure affecting all indexed contracts. Inflation forecasts are already proving optimistic, and the council's contingency appears insufficient.
findings.figures: Each additional 1% = approx. £0.750m across all three years
findings.quote: Inflation in 2025/26 and across the MTFS is higher than projections built into the budget. OBR October 2024 forecast is greater than MTFS assumptions. Each additional 1% equates to approx. £0.750m.

findings.headline: Pay award inflation carries £0.6m-£0.9m annual risk if wage settlements exceed 3% assumption
findings.detail: The council has assumed 3% pay award growth but notes pay awards are often set after the budget is finalised. Each additional 1% above the 3% assumption creates approximately £0.574m-£0.932m of unfunded pressure across the general fund.
findings.matters: Pay awards are largely fixed costs the council cannot defer. If actual settlements run higher, this is an immediate deficit pressure with no easy mitigation.
findings.quote: 3% has been allowed for, which is broadly in line with inflationary forecasts. The risk quantified is for general fund only, showing the impact of a further 1%

findings.headline: Adult Social Care fee inflation is running ahead of budget assumptions; 4-5% uplifts are already being signalled by the market
findings.detail: The council has allowed 3.6% for Adult Social Care provider fee uplifts but neighbouring authorities are indicating increases of 3-4%, with some reaching 5%. The register quantifies that a 4% uplift costs an additional £0.243m and a 5% uplift an additional £0.780m annually.
findings.matters: This is a demand-led spend where the council has no discretion. If market pressures force uplift rates above the 3.6% assumption, the council faces unbudgeted cost increases every year.
findings.figures: 3.6% built into budget; 4% uplift = £0.243m additional cost; 5% uplift = £0.780m additional cost
findings.quote: Inflation has been estimated at 3.6% for 2026/27. Neighbouring authorities have indicated fee uplifts between 3% to 4%. An increase to 4% & 5% equates to an annual estimated risk of £0.243m and £0.780m respectively.

findings.headline: Council uses interim staff at approximately 3% of staffing budget (£2m annually) due to difficulty filling permanent positions
findings.detail: The council is unable to fill permanent positions and is forced to use more expensive interim staff. The register quantifies this as approximately 3% of the staffing budget, calculated at £2m annually. The council describes this as a persistent risk for 'critical or hard-to-fill posts.'
findings.matters: This represents a structural cost pressure arising from recruitment difficulty. It is not a one-off; it is built into the financial outlook as a recurring risk for all three years.
findings.figures: £2.000m per year (2026/27, 2027/28, 2028/29); approximately 3% of staffing budget
findings.quote: for critical or hard-to-fill posts, a risk remains that interim staff will cost more than their permanent equivalent. Indicative risk calculated as c.3% of staffing budget.

findings.headline: Three council-owned entities carry £5m annual risk, with only £3.3m (54%) provisioned
findings.detail: Council subsidiaries (JEH, GRE5, SCF) have retained losses creating a £5m annual underwriting risk to the general fund. The council has only set aside £3.3m in provision, representing 25.4% of the total risk exposure. The register notes further work is required as part of 2025/26 accounts closure.
findings.matters: This is a contingent liability that could crystallise if any subsidiary deteriorates. The underprovisioning means the council's stated reserves do not reflect the full exposure.
findings.figures: £5.000m per year (2026/27, 2027/28, 2028/29); £3.3m provision represents 25.4% of risk
findings.quote: To date £3.3m has been set aside in a provision and contribution for 2024/25 - this represents 25.4% of company risk.

findings.headline: High-delivery-risk savings totalling £6.6m by 2028/29 depend on policy changes and consultation processes that are not yet agreed
findings.detail: The council's savings plan includes £1.4m of high-risk savings in year 1, escalating to £6.6m by 2028/29. The risk register describes these as dependent on 'a policy change and / or implementing new technology / processes and / or consultation' — none of which are certain to complete or land on time.
findings.matters: These are large, material savings with acknowledged execution risk. If they do not land, the council will face an additional deficit equal to the shortfall, with no offsetting mitigation identified.
findings.quote: Non delivery of savings High (The approach to delivery is dependent on either a policy change and / or implementing new technology / processes and / or consultation)

findings.headline: SEND funding cliff-edge risk: 25% probability government will withdraw Safety Valve support from 2027/28, creating £13m-£16.75m annual funding gap
findings.detail: Slough has entered a Safety Valve Agreement with the Department for Education to manage its Special Educational Needs and Disability deficit. The risk register assumes a 25% probability this agreement ends from 2027/28, which would eliminate government funding support. The risk escalates from £3.1m to £16.75m by 2028/29. Additionally, there is an unquantified risk around 'DfE's future treatment of the accumulated deficit, which cannot be quantified at this stage.'
findings.matters: This is a conditional funding arrangement with the government. Loss of the agreement combined with mandatory SEND spending creates an unfunded liability on top of core deficits. The council cannot refuse the placements.
findings.figures: £3.100m (2026/27), £13.000m (2027/28), £16.750m (2028/29); 25% probability of statutory override discontinuation
findings.quote: The council has entered into a Safety Valve Agreement (SVA). Therefore as well as impacting on the overall council budget position, a significantly higher level of SEND spending could threaten the additional funding being offered... 25% probability assumed on statutory override discontinuation from 2027/28 onwards.

findings.headline: Five high-cost children's placements already put the budget under uncontrollable pressure
findings.detail: New placements at £20,000 per week have created a structural budget pressure rated Red. The council states this will 'put a pressure on the contract fee that may not be containable' — meaning if those children remain in placement, the cost cannot be absorbed.
findings.matters: These are not contingent costs; they are current commitments. Five children at this rate cost c.£5m annually with no mitigation available. This is a locked-in obligation.
findings.figures: £5.000m per year (2026/27, 2027/28, 2028/29); approximately £20k per week per child
findings.quote: A small number of children costing c.£20k per week have joined recently. If these placements continue, it will put a pressure on the contract fee that may not be containable.

findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation demand could exceed the £3m annual budget provision
findings.detail: The council has rebased the budget to 1,300 households but identified planned savings that explicitly require demand reduction to be affordable. Each 1% additional demand adds approximately £150,000. The council has flagged this as a Red (critical) risk.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a statutory duty but the council's financial plan depends on demand not growing. A 20% overshoot would consume the entire £3m allocation, forcing cuts elsewhere or requiring additional borrowing.
findings.figures: £3.000m per year (2026/27, 2027/28, 2028/29); 1,300 households; each 1% increase = c.£150k
findings.quote: The budget has been rebased to 1,300 households, but there are planned savings which require a reduction in demand. Each 1% demand increase would add c. £150k.

findings.headline: SEND inspection found 'widespread and/or systemic failings'; council requesting up to £1.4m virement to clear backlog
findings.detail: Local Area SEND inspection in 2025 identified systemic failures. Council proposes £1.4m investment in 2026/27 (£1.0m permanent, £0.4m early intervention) to strengthen statutory service and clear EHCP backlog. This is in addition to the £17.083m DSG deficit and reflects need for service reform not yet costed.
findings.matters: Systemic SEND failures expose council to intervention risk and legal challenge. The investment is one-off but signals underlying service fragility. Combined with growing DSG deficit, SEND is becoming increasingly difficult to manage.
findings.figures: SEND investment requested: up to £1.4m in 2026/27; permanent staffing increase 24 to 53 FTE (permanent cost rising to £0.5m); backlog team: 12 FTEs for 9 months (£0.7m one-off)
findings.quote: The SEND recovery investment required for 2026/27 is estimated to be up to £1.4m, depending on Government funding. £1.0m of this relates to the statutory service and backlog reduction, with the remaining £0.4m relating to early intervention and transformation.

findings.headline: Council still dependent on £15.709m Exceptional Financial Support with no clarity on end date beyond 2028/29
findings.detail: Council cannot achieve revenue balance without £15.709m government support. MTFS signals end of EFS by 2028/29 but requires delivery of multi-year savings plans already underperforming. If savings do not materialize, council will need to request extension or face further reserve depletion.
findings.matters: Reliance on Exceptional Financial Support limits council's autonomy and refinancing optionality. Any setback in savings delivery or demand control will force return to government for extensions, undermining creditworthiness. Lenders need confidence in genuine path to EFS exit.
findings.figures: 2025-26 EFS: £15.709m (unchanged from Q3); MTFS signals end of EFS by 2028/29; Council on direction under Local Government Act 2003 s.28 and s.15 of 1999 Act
findings.quote: The Council's MTFS rebuilds the General Fund towards a sustainable position and signals the end of Exceptional Financial Support by 2028/29, Work is underway to deliver the savings necessary to deliver the MTFS and a refreshed set of assumptions will be reported to Cabinet in July.

findings.headline: Asset disposal target of £79.4m over 3 years is critical to debt repayment strategy but 2025-26 delivered only £2.245m
findings.detail: Council assumed £21.7m in disposals for 2025-26 and 2027-28 in Treasury strategy but revised up to £79.4m across 2026-29 as basis for debt repayment plan. Actual 2025-26 result was £2.245m due to 'challenging market conditions, service need and issues arising through internal due diligence'. Without hitting disposal targets, council will need to borrow more, increasing debt and financing costs.
findings.matters: The entire debt repayment strategy depends on asset sales that are falling short. Slippage means more reliance on borrowing and higher financing costs in tight budget. Market conditions and delays suggest targets are aspirational, not firm.
findings.figures: Treasury assumed £21.7m disposals 2025-28, revised to £79.4m across 2026-29; 2025-26 actual: £2.245m (10% of original assumption); HRA disposals: £13.396m, of which £6.367m applied to General Fund per no-detriment policy; £8.7m GF disposal receipts applied to Capitalisation Direction
findings.quote: Receipts generated from General Fund asset disposals are necessary to finance the Exceptional Financial Support and mitigate debt costs arising from the CD. If the Council cannot achieve the required disposals, it will need to borrow more to finance the CD, increased external borrowing leads to additional capital financing costs, putting further unbudgeted pressure on the future year's revenue budgets as well as putting the Council behind against the published debt repayment strategy.

findings.headline: Sundry and adult social care debt reached £35.923m; bad debt provision at £5.610m
findings.detail: Outstanding debt from council services (including adult social care) totals £35.923m. Of this, £26.809m is not yet due, but £3.715m is over 366 days old. Bad debt provision calculated at £5.610m (5.6% of debt), close to the £5.604m held. This suggests material amounts at risk of non-collection, particularly from vulnerable service users.
findings.matters: Large debt book, especially from adult social care, reflects vulnerable individuals unable to pay assessed charges. Collection risk is high, and provisions may be insufficient if economic distress worsens. Non-collection reduces effective income and pressures reserves.
findings.figures: Total sundry and ASC debt: £35.923m; over 366 days old: £3.715m; 90-365 days: £1.152m + £0.321m; provision required: £5.610m vs held: £5.604m (increase of £0.006m)
findings.quote: As of the 31 of March 2026 the balance outstanding for Sundry Debts was £35.923m. Applying the formula used to estimate the level of provision required suggests this requires a provision of £5.610m. The current provision is £5.604m.

findings.headline: Council Tax collection at 93.19% (1.81% behind target); Business Rates at 95.47% (3.53% behind)
findings.detail: Both main tax sources underperforming against targets and prior year. Council Tax 1.81% behind target equates to £1.875m shortfall; residents continue struggling with cost-of-living. Business Rates collection down by £2.721m in cash terms, partly due to a £4.726m increase in Net Collectable Debit in Jan-March 2026 not allowing businesses time to pay.
findings.matters: Deteriorating collection signals resident and business payment distress. Business Rates collection weakness is particularly concerning as it may indicate economic stress in Slough's business base. These shortfalls defer income to 2026/27 when cash is already tight.
findings.figures: Council Tax collected: 93.19% (target 95%, 1.81% = £1.875m shortfall); 1.02% behind March 2025; Business Rates collected: 95.47% (target 99%, 3.53% = £4.905m shortfall); behind March 2025 by £2.721m cash
findings.quote: At the end of March 2026 in respect of in-year Council Tax, collection is 93.19% (1.81% behind target), and 1.02% behind the March 2025 position of 94.21%. 1.81% behind target equals £1.875m in cash terms. Residents continue to struggle with cost-of-living increases, and only two of the Berkshire Councils are ahead of where they were at the same point in 2024/25.

findings.headline: DSG cumulative deficit grew to £17.083m; High Needs Stability Grant only writes off 90% of historic deficit
findings.detail: Schools DSG ended year with £17.083m cumulative deficit (up from £10.489m). Government's High Needs Stability Grant (HNSG), if granted, will write off 90% of cumulative historic overspend (£13.323m) but leaves material residual deficit. DSG forecast to worsen further by £7.778m in 2026/27 to £24.861m.
findings.matters: DSG is ringfenced and legally cannot be offset against general fund. Growing DSG deficit locks in future pressures and reduces flexibility. Even with HNSG relief, Slough's High Needs Block is permanently in overspend and reforms are not yet implemented.
findings.figures: DSG deficit end 2025-26: £17.083m cumulative; in-year overspend £9.834m before Safety Valve (£6.594m after); forecast 2026-27 overspend: £7.778m leading to £24.861m cumulative; HNSG estimated at £13.323m but does not prevent future overspend
findings.quote: The cumulative DSG deficit is £17.083m and should the Council be eligible for the High Needs Stability Grant to support with 90% of the historic high needs DSG deficits, it should be noted that a material underlying DSG deficit will remain.

findings.headline: Only 64% of planned £11.8m savings achieved; £4.226m unachieved
findings.detail: Multiple directorate savings programmes underdelivered. Adults Services achieved only 66% of savings due to fairer charging delays and inability to identify high-cost placements for reduction. RHE achieved 51%. This signals savings targets are not realistic or management cannot execute them reliably.
findings.matters: Unachieved savings undermine credibility of MTFS projections. If savings are built into 2026/27 and 2027/28 budgets but not delivered, the council will face larger deficits than forecast. Lenders rely on MTFS credibility.
findings.figures: £7.579m achieved of £11.805m (64.2%); £4.226m unachieved (35.8%), with significant black-rated (unachievable) items totalling £4.226m by year-end
findings.quote: Progress on savings delivery for 2025/26 did not develop as quickly as was initially planned but there are some areas in which progress can be shown. Of the savings identified, c£7.5M (64%) are achieved and included in the outturn position.

findings.headline: £1.836m overspend on Slough Children First; contract renegotiation underway
findings.detail: Children's social care overspend driven by 7 new residential placements at £83k/week combined cost, plus higher legal costs. Council in discussions to adjust contract terms. This is a second major demand pressure after TA, signalling staffing and placement costs are out of line with budget assumptions.
findings.matters: Indicates the council cannot deliver children's services at forecast cost. Unresolved contract disputes create budget uncertainty for 2026/27 and beyond, and persistent overspend suggests underlying demand or unit costs are misjudged.
findings.figures: £1.836m overspend on SCF contract; 7 children in new residential placements costing £83k/week combined; underachievement of £0.255m on residential placement savings
findings.quote: 7 children have newly entered residential placements, only 1 of whom was previously in care in an inhouse foster placement. Their combined weekly costs are £83k; which on average would amount to £616k per annum per placement if they remained in the placement for a whole year.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs spiralled to £13.8m overspend, the sole driver of deficit
findings.detail: Housing subsidy loss on temporary accommodation accounts for almost the entire overspend. The council notes this is demand-driven, with residents struggling with cost-of-living increases. Without mitigation elsewhere, TA would have produced a £20.8m overspend.
findings.matters: TA overspend is not controllable through efficiency—it's a statutory duty driven by homelessness levels. If costs stay elevated, the council cannot balance without reserves or government support indefinitely.
findings.figures: £13.8m overspend on TA and Housing Benefit subsidy loss (offset by £1m other HB surpluses = £12.8m net); this alone was 97% of the £13.152m deficit
findings.quote: Temporary Accommodation and associated Housing Benefit Subsidy loss on TA - £13.8m (offset by £1m of other surpluses in Housing Benefit).

findings.headline: Reserves depleted to unsustainably low levels after £13.152m drawdown
findings.detail: General Fund reserves fall to £11.313m after using the full overspend to reduce reported deficit. Commissioners explicitly state the level is 'considered low' and flag risks to absorb in-year pressures or shocks. The council is losing its only buffer against unforeseen events.
findings.matters: Depleted reserves signal the council cannot absorb another year like this without cutting services or failing statutory duties. It weakens negotiating position with government and raises refinancing risk.
findings.figures: General reserve reduced from £23.465m to £11.313m after £13.152m drawdown; commissioners assess this as 'low'
findings.quote: The current general reserve level following the proposed drawdown is considered low. The position was anticipated and action to address this and build resilience to absorb in year pressures or future shocks is outlined in the 2026/27 MTFS.

findings.paper_title: Appx SOA 24-25 Debrief - Audit work and Sector Update March 2026
findings.headline: Any SEND cumulative deficits accumulated by 31 March 2028 will remain with the council when government takes over SEND funding on 1 April 2028
findings.detail: The 26 November 2025 Budget announced that central government will manage SEND costs from 1 April 2028 when statutory override ends. However, the announcement explicitly states 'Cumulative deficits at this point will remain with the relevant councils,' creating a cliff-edge deadline for Slough to eliminate or manage down its SEND deficit.
findings.matters: If Slough has a significant SEND deficit on 31 March 2028, it will absorb that loss into reserves or require unexpected spending cuts, reducing financial flexibility and potentially triggering borrowing needs.
findings.figures: Cliff-edge date: 31 March 2028; government takeover: 1 April 2028
findings.quote: Future Special Educational Needs and Disabilities (SEND) costs are to be managed by government once the statutory override ends on 31st March 2028. Cumulative deficits at this point will remain with the relevant councils.

findings.paper_title: Appx SOA 24-25 Debrief - Audit work and Sector Update March 2026
findings.headline: Significant staff turnover has eroded control effectiveness, including loss of expertise in managing £3.382 million suspense account balance
findings.detail: Auditor noted 'significant changes to staff' since the last full audit. Broader controls do not appear to be operating as effectively as previously. The council previously had third-party assistance reviewing suspense accounts but 'following the departure of staff previously involved with the work, there is no ongoing review process to resolve and clear suspense items.'
findings.matters: Loss of finance team expertise increases the risk of recurring control weaknesses, slower resolution of audit findings, and higher external advisory costs to rebuild capability.
findings.figures: No specific headcount, but loss of suspense account review capacity noted
findings.quote: It has been some time since a full audit process was completed and there have been significant changes to staff. As such some of the broader controls that have previously been in place do not appear to be operating as effectively as possible

findings.paper_title: Appx SOA 24-25 Debrief - Audit work and Sector Update March 2026
findings.headline: Transaction testing of 231 items found only 49% passed with no audit queries, while 9 items were incorrectly classified and 2 items worth £51k were not accrued
findings.detail: Of 39 fees and charges tested, 24 raised queries and 9 were incorrectly mapped as fees when should be grant income. Of 52 grant income items tested, 30 raised queries. Of 105 operating expenditure items, 46 raised queries. Expenditure completeness testing found 2 items totalling £51k that should have been accrued for 2024/25 but were not.
findings.matters: High failure rates in transaction testing indicate systemic weaknesses in transaction recording, classification and completeness that undermine the reliability of management accounts and year-end financial statements.
findings.figures: 231 items tested; 114 passed (49%); 103 raised queries; 9 incorrectly classified; 2 accruals of £51k missing
findings.quote: Much of this was provided by the central finance team and, to further improve the process, the council should seek further involvement of service teams to ensure the information provided is complete and suitable for audit

findings.paper_title: Appx SOA 24-25 Debrief - Audit work and Sector Update March 2026
findings.headline: 122 distinct points identified requiring improvement in financial statement disclosures, particularly on exceptional financial support and capitalisation directives
findings.detail: Audit review found inadequate disclosure of receipt, use and financing of exceptional financial support and capitalisation directions; incorrect classification of government grants as ring-fenced vs non-ring-fenced; and deficient disclosures of financial instruments, fair value of assets, and infrastructure assets. Auditor recommends council complete CIPFA disclosure checklist for 2025/26.
findings.matters: Clear, compliant disclosure of exceptional support arrangements is essential for lenders to assess the conditionality of government support, potential repayment obligations, and sustainability of the council's financial position.
findings.figures: 122 lines of follow-up and improvement identified
findings.quote: We identified a number of points to be addressed within the Council's financial statements. We would recommend that, as part of its accounts preparation process, the Council complete the Cipfa disclosure checklist to aid in the preparation of a code compliant set of financial statements

findings.paper_title: Appx SOA 24-25 Debrief - Audit work and Sector Update March 2026
findings.headline: £1.9 million unexplained difference between payroll system and employee benefits expenditure in financial statements
findings.detail: Payroll-to-financial statements reconciliation is not part of routine procedures. While some variance explained by schools' own payroll arrangements, the largest single difference of £1.9 million could not be explained within audit timescales, suggesting either missing costs or misclassification in one of the council's largest budget categories.
findings.matters: Unexplained payroll variances of this magnitude indicate potential gaps in employee cost recording, a material budget area that directly affects service delivery capacity and genuine operating costs.
findings.figures: £1.9 million unexplained variance
findings.quote: The reconciliation identified a number of differences, the largest being £1.9m, which in the time available could not be fully explained.

findings.paper_title: Appx SOA 24-25 Debrief - Audit work and Sector Update March 2026
findings.headline: £3.382 million in uncleared suspense accounts with no regular review process and £3.123 million variance from trial balance
findings.detail: Suspense accounts contain unmatched income with entries covering multiple periods, including balances dating to 2015. There are significant debit and credit entries that have not been regularly reviewed or cleared. The council previously relied on third-party assistance to manage suspense accounts but has no ongoing review process following staff departures. Some balances are mis-dated (2033, 2047).
findings.matters: Large unreconciled suspense balances cloud the actual financial position, distort receivables figures, and indicate weak cash and income controls that lenders must assess when evaluating repayment capacity.
findings.figures: £3.382 million net value in suspense accounts; £3.123 million variance between suspense accounts and trial balance
findings.quote: Individual suspense account include some old balances (2015) indicating these have not been regularly reviewed

findings.paper_title: Appx SOA 24-25 Debrief - Audit work and Sector Update March 2026
findings.headline: Slough received a disclaimer of opinion on 2024/25 accounts because the council could not produce financial statements and supporting papers within agreed timescales
findings.detail: Despite stated best efforts, the council was unable to produce accounts and necessary working papers to meet agreed audit deadlines. Draft statements were only published 12 December 2025, leaving insufficient time for a full audit, resulting in a disclaimed opinion on 2024/25 statements. This follows disclaimed opinions on all years up to and including 2023/24.
findings.matters: Audit disclaimers prevent lenders and stakeholders from forming a verified view of the council's financial position and underlying asset quality, increasing borrowing costs and limiting access to credit markets.
findings.figures: Disclaimer of opinion on 2024/25 financial statements; all years up to 31 March 2024 also disclaimed
findings.quote: However, as the financial statements for the outstanding years were finalised, it became apparent that despite its best efforts the Council would be unable to produce accounts and necessary supporting working papers in line with our agreed timetable for the draft financial statements.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Budget and MTFS Report to Council, 26th February 2026
findings.headline: Council Tax increase of 4.99% (2.99% general plus 2% Adult Social Care precept) assumed to balance budget
findings.detail: The proposed balanced budget is based on a 4.99% increase in Council Tax: 2.99% on the general element and 2% on the Adult Social Care precept. This is at the top of the permitted level without referendum. The budget also assumes Council Tax base growth of c.0.5% per year and a collection rate of 98.25%.
findings.matters: The budget depends on maximum Council Tax rises and optimistic collection assumptions; any shortfall in either collection or base growth would create additional budget pressure requiring reserve drawdown or further savings.
findings.figures: 4.99% (total Council Tax increase), 2.99% (general element), 2% (ASC precept), c.0.5% (assumed tax base growth per year), 98.25% (collection rate assumption)
findings.quote: The proposed balanced budget is based upon a 4.99% increase in Council Tax and subject to Exceptional Financial Support for 2026/27 of £42.9m – in the form of a capitalisation direction to be approved by government... an increase in the general element of the council tax of 2.99% and an increase in the Adult Social Care Precept element of 2%, totalling 4.99%.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Budget and MTFS Report to Council, 26th February 2026
findings.headline: Capital borrowing requirements: £65.3m EFS plus £20m transformation plus £20.2m essential capex over 5 years
findings.detail: Beyond the revenue EFS, the council requires £65.3m borrowing across the MTFS to fund capitalisation direction, £20m capital investment in transformation, and £20.2m essential capital expenditure over the capital programme period. Borrowing costs are spread over 20 years for EFS and the useful life of assets for capital.
findings.matters: Total borrowing requirements approach £105m+ above EFS, materially increasing the council's debt position and future capital financing costs over a generation.
findings.figures: £65.3m (EFS borrowing across MTFS), £20m (transformation capital investment), £20.2m (essential capex over 5 years)
findings.quote: The Treasury Management Strategy assumes the Council is allowed to borrow up to £65.3m across the MTFS to enable the Council to be financially sustainable without the requirement for EFS in 2028/29. There is also a requirement for the Council to borrow £20m to fund capital investment in transformation and £20.2m to fund essential capital expenditure over the five years of the capital programme.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Budget and MTFS Report to Council, 26th February 2026
findings.headline: Accounts not audited since 2018/19; six years of catch-up work only recently completed
findings.detail: The council's statement of accounts has not been audited since 2018/19 due to historical challenges with working papers and data availability. Over the past 18 months, six sets of accounts (up to 2024/25) have been prepared and external support commissioned to review the balance sheet. This represents a significant historical governance and audit control gap.
findings.matters: A multi-year audit backlog signals weak financial control and raises uncertainty about the accuracy and reliability of historical financial data; lack of audited accounts complicates covenant compliance and due diligence.
findings.figures: 0 audited accounts (2018/19 to 2025/26), 6 sets prepared (2018/19 to 2024/25) in last 18 months
findings.quote: The Council's statement of accounts has not been audited since 2018/19 due to accounts not being produced on time as a result of historical challenges with working papers and availability of financial data. This has been addressed over the past 18 months with six sets of accounts having been prepared, up to and including 2024/25 financial year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Budget and MTFS Report to Council, 26th February 2026
findings.headline: Grant Thornton has signalled auditor concerns on financial sustainability given DSG deficit trajectory
findings.detail: Grant Thornton (external auditor) has indicated that total usable reserves should exceed the level of any accumulated deficit to demonstrate financial sustainability. The council acknowledges it expects the DSG deficit to exceed available reserves by 2027/28 if the financial position is not significantly changed. This represents a forward warning from the auditor of potential sustainability concerns.
findings.matters: Auditor concern about reserve adequacy relative to deficit size is a governance warning; if the auditor escalates to an adverse opinion on financial sustainability, it signals material financial distress.
findings.figures: £25m (DSG deficit 2026/27), potentially above £50m (2027/28)
findings.quote: the Council's auditor Grant Thornton has indicated that total usable reserves should exceed the level of the deficit in order to demonstrate financial sustainability from their perspective (although it is noted that some councils with deficits already considerably in excess of total usable reserves have not received adverse comments concerning financial sustainability from their auditors). The Council expects the deficit to exceed available reserves by 2027/28 if the financial position is not significantly changed by expected announcements on tackling DSG spending and funding future deficits.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Budget and MTFS Report to Council, 26th February 2026
findings.headline: Adults Social Care demand materially above benchmark: 1,235 clients aged 65+ vs. 794–1,074 for comparators
findings.detail: Slough has 1,235 clients aged 65+ against unitary authority benchmark of 794 and London Borough benchmark of 1,074. The average cost per client is £19,583. The council plans £5m savings in Adults over the MTFS, but the underlying demand position suggests structural oversupply of services relative to comparable authorities.
findings.matters: Disproportionately high demand for adult social care indicates either demographic risk, service model inefficiency, or prevention failures; if demand continues to grow, it will pressure the savings plan.
findings.figures: 1,235 (Slough clients aged 65+), 794 (Unitary benchmark), 1,074 (London Borough benchmark), £19,583 (average cost per client), £5m (planned savings over MTFS)
findings.quote: At the time of the benchmarking work Slough had 1,235 clients aged 65+ throughout the year. This compares to a range of 794 (Unitaries) and 1,074 (London Boroughs). Total savings in Adults of £5m are set out over the Medium-Term. Adults aged 65+ - Slough average cost £19,583 against a benchmark for Unitary Authorities of £20,640.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Budget and MTFS Report to Council, 26th February 2026
findings.headline: Slough Children First contract volatile: placement costs c.£20k per week; five additional children could create £5m unbudgeted pressure
findings.detail: The contract with Slough Children First increases by £1.162m to £39.517m for 2026/27. The council notes that placement costs are highly sensitive to small changes in demand. Five additional children placed at average cost of c.£20k per week would create an illustrative pressure of up to £5m, not currently in the budget and would need to be met from contingency and/or reserves.
findings.matters: Volatile children's social care costs create unquantified budget risk; a small deterioration in case complexity or placement needs could exhaust remaining contingency and trigger reserve depletion.
findings.figures: £39.517m (Slough Children First contract 2026/27), £1.162m (increase), c.£20k per week (average placement cost), £5m (illustrative pressure for 5 additional high-cost placements)
findings.quote: for example, children for whom placements can cost c.£20k per week on average. Placing just 5 children at this level would lead to an illustrative pressure of up to £5m, which is not currently explicitly part of the budget and would need to be met from contingency and/or reserves if additional funding for the company was agreed by the Council.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Budget and MTFS Report to Council, 26th February 2026
findings.headline: Inflation risk: CPI at 3.4% vs. budget assumption of 2–3%, creating potential £1.3m annual pressure
findings.detail: The budget assumes pay award of 3% for 2026/27 and 2% for 2027/28 and 2028/29. However, ONS CPI rose to 3.4% in January 2026. The Section 151 Officer states that increasing inflation assumptions by 1% would create an additional pressure of c.£1.3m per year over the three-year MTFS, a material risk if the current trajectory continues.
findings.matters: Inflation assumptions are already tightening; if inflation remains above budget, the council faces additional unplanned pressures that would need to be met from contingency or trigger further savings requirements.
findings.figures: 3.4% (CPI as at 21 January 2026), 3% (pay award assumption 2026/27), 2% (pay award assumptions 2027/28–2028/29), £1.3m (annual pressure per 1% increase)

findings.matters: A S114 notice is a public declaration of financial failure. It is rare, serious, and material to credit assessment. The fact that the council remains in this state (albeit with government life-support) is a key marker of structural vulnerability.
