findings.headline: Weighted risk assessment shows reserves only marginally cover assessed financial exposure
findings.detail: The council's formal risk assessment calculates £37.107m of weighted financial risk across funding, inflation, demand, savings delivery, companies, corporate and financing costs. The assumed level of general and non-restricted reserves by 2028/29 is only £33.564m — a shortfall before adding any new risks or if any risks materialise at the top end of the range.
findings.matters: A lender assesses whether a council has sufficient buffers for normal business volatility. This council's assessed risk nearly exceeds its planned reserve buffer, leaving very little room for adverse variance.
findings.figures: Weighted risk: £37.107m; assumed general + non-restricted reserves 2028/29: £33.564m
findings.quote: An assessment of current budget risks and sensitivities is set in the table below. It reflects the assessment of financial risks for the year 2028/29... This is compared to the estimated level of General and non-restricted earmarked reserves.

findings.headline: Council cannot manage demand-led cost growth and depends on exceptional government support
findings.detail: Slough explicitly states it lacks resources to meet demand pressures in homelessness, adult social care, children's social care and SEND. The council is dependent on Capitalisation Directions (exceptional financial support) totalling £336.5m to date and £417.5m forecast to 2027/28 just to balance the budget. The budget will not hold without this support.
findings.matters: A lender cannot assume this council is self-correcting. If government support ends before the spending pressures are resolved, the council will either need further support, make politically difficult service reductions, or breach its budget.
findings.quote: This reflects the fact that the authority does not have the level of resources to manage the impact of the scale of growth in demand-led services, primarily homelessness, adult social care, children's social care and SEND.

findings.headline: General Fund reserves forecast to hit only £8.972m by end 2025/26, down from £23.465m at start of year
findings.detail: The council's main revenue reserve is being depleted at speed. The 2025/26 estimated overspend of £15.493m (as at December 2025) is driving reserves down to a level the council itself describes as inadequate. This follows a wider fall from £69.2m in 2023 to £43.4m in 2025.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the trajectory of the council's cash resilience. A reserve falling this steeply, and this low relative to net revenue budget, signals limited capacity to absorb further shocks without further external support.
findings.figures: General Reserve opening 2025/26: £23.465m; forecast closing: £8.972m; overspend: £15.493m
findings.quote: By the end of the 2025/26 financial year, the General Reserve is forecast to reduce to £8.972m, following an estimated GF overspend of £15.493m (as at end December 2025).

findings.headline: DSG deficit will hit the revenue account in 2027/28 when statutory override expires
findings.detail: Slough holds a £25.4m DSG deficit in unusable reserves under a statutory override that is time-limited to 2027/28. Once the override ends, this becomes a charge to the revenue account — a material shock to finances that the council has not yet funded. The deficit is driven primarily by the growing cost of SEND statutory responsibilities.
findings.matters: A lender evaluating covenant strength needs to know whether this council can absorb a £25m hit to revenue when the override expires, or whether it will require further government intervention.
findings.figures: £25.4m DSG deficit; statutory override ends 2027/28
findings.quote: As is the case in many local authorities the DSG for Slough is in significant deficit, primarily as a consequence of the increased and growing cost of SEND statutory responsibilities. The statutory override is time limited to 2027/28, and this represents a significant risk to the Council.

findings.headline: Minimal cash reserves of £13.6m and high reliance on internal borrowing (£187.3m) to fund operations
findings.detail: The council holds only £13.6m in cash investments as of 31 December 2025, expected to fluctuate between £10m and £50m in 2026/27. To bridge the gap between actual borrowing and capital financing requirement, the council relies on £187.3m of internal borrowing (drawing down reserves and other balance sheet resources). This leaves little buffer for unexpected costs and will force increased external borrowing as internal resources deplete.
findings.matters: Thin liquidity leaves the council vulnerable to cash flow disruptions. Heavy reliance on internal borrowing means reserves are being depleted to fund ongoing operations rather than held for resilience. As internal resources shrink over the forecast period, external borrowing will rise, increasing refinancing risk and costs.
findings.figures: Cash investments 31 Dec 2025: £13.6m; forecast range 2026/27: £10m-£50m; internal borrowing 2026/27: £187.3m; total CFR £699.3m
findings.quote: At 31st December 2025, the Council held £13.6m in invested funds, representing income received in advance of expenditure plus balances and reserves.

findings.headline: Financial plan depends on achieving £79.4m asset disposal receipts between 2026/27 and 2028/29
findings.detail: Slough's strategy to exit EFS by 2028/29 relies on disposing of £79.4m of assets over the three-year period, with proceeds used to reduce borrowing requirements and fund capital transformation investment (£20m). Any shortfall in disposals—due to market conditions, property valuations, or regulatory delays—would force additional borrowing or cuts to capital spending.
findings.matters: Asset disposal targets are a critical assumption in the council's financial recovery plan. Market risk, property valuations, and planning constraints could all affect delivery. Failure to achieve targets would undermine the case for exiting EFS support.
findings.figures: £79.4m asset disposals planned 2026/27-2028/29; £227.8m disposals achieved in 2025/26; £307.2m cumulative disposals 2018/19-2028/29
findings.quote: In line with the previous EFS agreement, the council will look to use disposal receipts to reduce the level of borrowing required. Over the period 2026/27 to 2028/29 £79.4m of disposal receipts are expected which will be used to reduce the level of borrowing detailed above.

findings.headline: Council requesting £65.3m additional Exceptional Financial Support from MHCLG for 2026/27 and 2027/28, extending government rescue package
findings.detail: Five years after issuing a section 114 notice (July 2021), Slough is requesting a further £65.3m of EFS to support revenue position through 2027/28. The council attributes this to ongoing structural pressures on temporary accommodation and adult social care, plus delayed income from fair funding reform. It plans to exit EFS by 2028/29.
findings.matters: The request for additional support despite being five years into recovery indicates the underlying deficit is structural, not temporary. Ongoing demand pressures and delayed reform income raise questions about the realism of the 2028/29 exit plan.
findings.figures: £65.3m additional EFS requested for 2026/27 and 2027/28; originally agreed EFS was £352.2m until end 2025/26; £91.6m EFS utilised by end 2025/26
findings.quote: The ongoing recurrent demand pressures on service such as temporary accommodation (TA) and Adult Social Care (ASC) during 2025/26 as well as the delayed full receipt of additional income to Slough as part of the fair funding reform means that the Council has requested from Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) £65.3m of EFS to support the Council's revenue position in 2026/27 and 2027/28.

findings.headline: Council faces constrained access to external finance due to credit concerns, relying solely on PWLB for new borrowing
findings.detail: The treasury strategy explicitly states that access to finance is constrained by perceived credit concerns about Slough, limiting borrowing options to the PWLB and ruling out capital markets or bank lending. This reflects market perception of credit risk.
findings.matters: Restricted access to finance limits the council's flexibility and may increase borrowing costs or force unpalatable choices between capital investment and debt repayment. It indicates market concern about financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £443.7m in loans held as of 31 Dec 2025 (down £14.8m from prior year); £112.9m new borrowing forecast for 2026/27; PWLB is only available source
findings.quote: However, access to finance may occasionally be constrained due to perceived credit concerns for Slough. Therefore, the PWLB will remain the Council's primary source of borrowing.

findings.headline: HRA operating with minimal reserves and tight interest cover ratio
findings.detail: HRA general reserves set at minimum £4m and Major Repairs Reserve at minimum £5m (£9m total) against £622m asset base. Interest cover ratio minimum is 1.25x, described as reflecting "national challenges HRA's face." These minimums are reviewed annually.
findings.matters: Minimal financial headroom (1.4% reserve coverage) for adverse developments; HRA vulnerable to cost inflation, void losses, or interest rate rises given tight position
findings.figures: £622m HRA asset base; £9m minimum total reserves; 7,372 tenanted units; 1.25x minimum interest cover ratio
findings.quote: The minimum HRA level of general reserves of £4m. The minimum level of Major Repairs Reserve of £5m. The minimum level should be 1.25 reflecting the national challenges HRA's face.

findings.headline: Capital schemes may be paused or aborted if revenue budget cannot be balanced through savings alone due to constrained borrowing capacity
findings.detail: Council explicitly identifies risk that schemes may be "paused/aborted" if revenue budget cannot be balanced through savings alone, since borrowing capacity is already heavily constrained by Commissioner. This creates contingency for budget pressures.
findings.matters: If revenue savings targets not achieved in any year, capital investment will be cut; creates uncertainty for services dependent on capital programme delivery
findings.figures: No specific schemes or amounts identified at risk
findings.quote: The Council may need to make additional savings to enable the budget to be balanced which may impact the ability to borrow to fund capital expenditure, this may mean certain schemes may need to be paused/aborted.

findings.headline: £84.7m of asset disposals planned as key funding source for capital programme
findings.detail: Council has run an asset disposal programme since 2022/23 aimed at rationalising its asset base. General Fund disposal receipts are specifically directed to reduce borrowing under the EFS agreement. Projected net receipts of £84.7m are planned over 2026/27-2029/30.
findings.matters: Material portion of General Fund capital funding (£179.5m over 5 years) depends on disposal timing and prices; shortfall creates funding gap that forces either borrowing increase (constrained by Commissioner) or deferrals of capital schemes
findings.figures: £84.7m disposals 2026/27-2029/30; £179.516m General Fund capital 2026/27-2030/31; proceeds used to reduce £85.332m Capital Direction borrowing

findings.headline: Debt reduction to peer average is mandatory condition of financial recovery
findings.detail: Council must reduce its debt level "to be comparable to the average for a unitary authority of a similar size and core funding level" within "a reasonable timescale." This is a condition of EFS. A separate Debt Repayment Strategy has been developed to drive the requirement.
findings.matters: Implies current debt materially exceeds peer level; forces debt reduction to take priority over service expansion in capital allocation decisions
findings.figures: Current debt level not disclosed; target is peer average for similar-sized authorities
findings.quote: The Capital Strategy for Slough Borough Council (SBC) must also align with the requirement for the Council to reduce its level of debt and associated capital financing charges over a reasonable timescale to be comparable to the average for a unitary authority of a similar size and core funding level.

findings.headline: Council operates under Exceptional Financial Support with Commissioner-imposed constraints on borrowing and capital spending
findings.detail: Slough has been under EFS since 2018/19 and must produce a refreshed Capital Strategy as condition of continued support. Secretary of State appointed commissioner provides advice and challenge to the Council with explicit mandate to "strictly limit" future borrowing and capital spending. This represents direct external constraint on capital flexibility.
findings.matters: EFS is public signal of financial distress; Commissioner oversight directly restricts the Council's ability to borrow for capital investment and limits discretionary spending
findings.figures: Capital Direction borrowing £85.332m, New Borrowing £20.182m planned for 2026/27-2030/31

findings.headline: Corporate & Cross Cutting savings rely on £4.8m of commercialisation and income generation proposals, most awaiting Cabinet approval
findings.detail: The council is planning £1.5m from fees and charges review (COR-TP-09, Cabinet approval pending), £0.75m from commercial/procurement management (COR-TP-08), £1.05m from strategic commissioning of homelessness (COR-TP-04), and £0.665m from solar/battery storage energy export (RHE-TP-10). Additional income is expected from parking charging optimization (£2.4m), registration service commercialisation (£0.55m), and S106 leveraging (£0.3m). Cabinet approval is pending on most of these.
findings.matters: Income-based savings often underdeliver when demand does not materialize or when service changes trigger customer resistance. A lender needs to know whether these are conservative estimates or optimistic projections. The fees and charges review in particular may face political or delivery friction.

findings.headline: Adult social care relies on commissioning/service redesign totalling £5.2m, with significant delivery dependencies on technology and reablement models
findings.detail: Adults savings of £5.19m over three years depend on: reviews of double-handed care (£0.7m), technology and decision-making dashboards (£0.8m), triage process redesign (£1.1m), mental health service review with NHS (£1.05m), and increased CHC applications (£0.9m with 1 FTE specialist social worker investment). Several of these require external partner agreement (Berkshire Healthcare NHS Trust) or depend on take-up of new digital/reablement services. The CHC programme is an invest-to-save requiring additional staffing.
findings.matters: ASC is the largest and most volatile budget area for councils. A lender needs visibility into whether these services can genuinely reduce demand or shift costs, or whether the council is betting on service redesign in an area with limited track record of rapid transformation. Dependency on technology adoption and external partners (NHS) adds delivery risk.

These represent scope and financial uncertainty.

A lender cannot assess the credibility of a plan when nearly a tenth of transformation spending is unscheduled.

findings.headline: Housing transformation assumes reduction of 'numbers of households in temporary accommodation' by £4.85m over three years, with staffing needs unconfirmed
findings.detail: RHE-TP-01 (Housing Demand & TA Service Transformation Programme) projects £0.85m (2026/27), £2.4m (2027/28), and £1.6m (2028/29) from reducing temporary accommodation cases. The document notes 'Additional staffing may be required on an invest to save basis' but does not confirm numbers or cost. Multiple related housing delivery programmes (lettings agency, modular, LAHF, adaptations) are bundled into the savings with similar caveats on unconfirmed staffing.
findings.matters: TA caseloads are structural drivers of council deficits across England. A lender needs to see evidence that the council can actually reduce placements, or faces significant downside risk if the programmes underdeliver. Unconfirmed staffing costs also represent hidden budget risk.

findings.headline: A structural deficit emerges in 2027/28 as a £4.4m one-off business rate gain falls away
findings.detail: The council's baseline savings plan shows a negative £2.928m gap in 2027/28, driven by loss of a one-off business rate collection improvement from 2025. The document notes this on the 2027/28 summary: "Business Rate collection improvement - one-off gain from Rateable Value finder exercise" valued at £4.431m in 2026/27 that does not recur. This means the council must find transformation savings just to replace a one-time gain.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council has a sustainable savings plan or is relying on one-off adjustments to mask structural imbalance. A £2.9m gap appearing once the one-off ends is a material signal.

findings.headline: Housing regulatory oversight: Regulator of Social Housing and Housing Ombudsman involved in service improvement plan
findings.detail: Housing Services is operating under a Service Improvement Plan overseen by the Regulator of Social Housing and Housing Ombudsman. The council explicitly aims to demonstrate compliance with Consumer Standards under the Social Housing Regulation Act 2023. This indicates regulatory intervention or monitoring.
findings.matters: Regulatory oversight of housing services signals compliance breaches or performance issues serious enough to attract regulator attention. This is a material governance risk and may indicate service failures (safety, repairs, communication) that could lead to enforcement action.

findings.detail: Across directorates, transformation savings of at least £5.682m are planned for 2026/27 (Adults £1.365m, Children's £1.417m, RHE £2.534m, Law & Governance £0.550m, Corporate Resources £1.350m) with total medium-term targets exceeding £15m. These are large structural changes. The document does not detail what happens if savings do not land.
findings.matters: Transformation savings of this scale are high-risk, dependent on successful service redesign and often face delays or delivery shortfalls. The council is heavily dependent on these to maintain financial balance, but the paper provides no detail on delivery mechanisms, timescales, or contingency if they slip.

This breadth of workstreams indicates systemic rather than isolated issues.
findings.matters: A finance improvement programme spanning nine workstreams covering basic functions (systems, controls, reconciliation, policies) suggests the council lacks fundamental financial control processes that would normally be baseline. This elevates operational risk.

Savings of only £2.310m are planned against total pressures. The budget risks column shows an additional £5.920m of pressure.

findings.detail: The Programmes and Change team (13 staff) delivering corporate transformation are funded from reserves allocated for change and transformation rather than from baseline budgets. This directly consumes reserves to cover improvement staff costs while the council attempts to restructure. Multiple improvement and recovery teams are running in parallel across directorates.
findings.matters: Using reserves to fund ongoing operational transformation activities (7 improvement, 6 operating model staff) is unsustainable and signals the council cannot afford these functions from core budget. Reserves exist for emergencies and one-offs, not permanent restructuring costs.

findings.headline: No full external audit of accounts for seven years; first audit since 2018/19 planned for 2025/26
findings.detail: The council has recently cleared a backlog in preparing financial statements for 2023/24 and 2024/25 after several years of delays and challenges. The 2025/26 accounts must be published by 30 June 2026 to enable a full audit to be undertaken — described as the council's first since 2018/19. This represents a significant gap in external financial scrutiny.
findings.matters: A seven-year gap without full audit oversight indicates serious financial control weaknesses and creates material uncertainty about the accuracy of prior accounts. A lender needs confidence in the council's financial reporting.

This is separate from a further £0.25m demographic growth pressure. Over three years the demand-based pressure alone is £15.3m.

findings.headline: Major transformation programme with £31.357m savings planned over three years, 66% dependent on housing and temporary accommodation reductions
findings.detail: Slough is pursuing a transformational savings approach with £5.248m in 2026/27, £10.595m in 2027/28, and £15.513m in 2028/29. Regeneration, Housing & Environment accounts for £20.593m of the total, heavily reliant on reducing temporary accommodation households and delivering new housing through LAHF match-funding (£5.5m), modular housing (£625k), a social lettings agency (£900k), and other housing delivery schemes.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that this scale of savings is credible. The heavy concentration in housing and TA demand reduction means the entire programme depends on achieving ambitious targets for reducing household numbers — a bet on external factors like housing delivery timing and demand pressures
findings.figures: Total: £31.357m. RHE: £20.593m (66%). Housing Demand & TA: £4.85m. LAHF: £5.5m. Housing Delivery schemes (modular, lettings agency, adaptations, grant funding): £3.95m. Parking & transport: £2.975m
findings.quote: Total Directorate Transformational Adults 3,997,000 Children 1,417,000 PHPP - RHE 20,593,000 L&G 550,000 Corporate & Cross Cutting 4,800,000 Total 31,357,000

findings.headline: Significant data quality gaps and lack of data-driven culture limiting service planning and decision-making
findings.detail: The Commissioners' July 2025 report identified lack of reliable data and absence of a data-driven culture as major barriers to progress. The Council's Annual Governance Statement acknowledges gaps in member-level reporting and inconsistent access to accurate data. The auditor notes the Council continues to face significant challenges in data quality and analytical capacity, particularly at service level, and that improvement plans are at an early stage.
findings.matters: Poor data quality undermines the Council's ability to plan budgets accurately, identify service problems early, or make informed spending decisions. This contributes to the budget forecast errors and in-year overspends evident in this year's position.
findings.figures: Data quality noted as major barrier by Commissioners; gaps in member reporting; inconsistent data access
findings.quote: The Commissioners' July 2025 report highlighted the lack of reliable data and a data-driven culture as major barriers to progress. While improvement plans are in place, they are at an early stage and depend on cultural change, investment in IT infrastructure, and retaining skilled staff.

findings.headline: Council remains under commissioners' intervention until November 2026; Chief Executive appointed to dual role as Managing Director Commissioner
findings.detail: The Council has been under commissioners' intervention since 2022. In October 2024, intervention was extended until November 2026 citing 'ongoing concerns about the Council's capacity to deliver efficient and economical services'. The Chief Executive was appointed to a dual role of Managing Director Commissioner to accelerate pace of change. The latest Commissioners' report (July 2025) acknowledged improvements but highlighted ongoing challenges.
findings.matters: Extended intervention signals the government has lost confidence in the Council's ability to self-correct. The high-level restructuring of senior leadership and need for external commissioner oversight indicates governance instability and execution risk.
findings.figures: Intervention extended to November 2026 (original from 2022); Chief Executive in dual management role
findings.quote: In October 2024, the Department for Levelling Up, Housing and Communities extended the intervention until November 2026, citing ongoing concerns about the Council's capacity to deliver efficient and economical services. The Council's Chief Executive was appointed to a dual role of Managing Director Commissioner to accelerate the pace of change.

findings.headline: Internal audit did not have effective arrangements in place during all of 2024/25, resulting in 'No Assurance' opinion for the year
findings.detail: The Council did not have effective internal audit arrangements in place during all of 2024/25. Following poor delivery up to November 2024, the Council appointed an interim external Head of Internal Audit. While this allowed a short-term plan to be delivered, internal audit issued a 'No Assurance' annual opinion for 2024/25, undermining wider assurance and improvement activity.
findings.matters: No assurance from internal audit, combined with a disclaimed external audit opinion, means the Council has no independent assurance on the adequacy of its internal controls or financial reporting. This is a red flag for any lender.
findings.figures: No Assurance opinion from internal audit for 2024/25; gap in effective arrangements during the year
findings.quote: The Council did not have effective internal audit arrangements in place during all of 2024/25, undermining wider assurance and improvement activity. The Council has acknowledged that more progress is required, recognising this as a key corporate risk.

findings.headline: Auditor unable to form opinion on 2024/25 financial statements and plans to issue disclaimer due to late publication and scope limitations
findings.detail: The draft 2024/25 accounts were not published until 12 December 2025, with no realistic possibility of conducting a full audit by the statutory deadline of 27 February 2026. Due to these delays and scope limitations, the auditor plans to issue a disclaimer of audit opinion on the financial statements. The Council also has ongoing weaknesses in books and records and internal control environment.
findings.matters: A disclaimer of audit opinion means no external assurance on the accuracy or completeness of the financial statements. Combined with noted weaknesses in records and controls, this creates high uncertainty about the true financial position.
findings.figures: Draft 2024/25 accounts published 12 December 2025 (vs 30 June 2025 requirement); statutory deadline 27 February 2026
findings.quote: The draft 2023/24 and 2024/25 accounts were not published until 31 October 2025 and 12 December 2025 respectively, meaning that there was no realistic possibility of conducting and completing our audit work by the statutory backstop deadline for each year. This means that the limitations of scope imposed by the backstop are pervasive and therefore we have been unable to form an opinion on the financial statements by the due date. We therefore plan to issue a disclaimer of the audit opinion for 2024/25.

findings.headline: Earmarked reserves drawn down by £11m (from £29.2m to £18m) to fund 2024/25 overspend; plan to build reserves depends on unachieved balanced budget
findings.detail: Earmarked reserves were reduced by £11 million (from £29.2 million to £18 million) to support the delivery of the 2024/25 budget and cover the Council's overspend. For 2025/26, the Council intends to transfer £1 million to reserves to build financial sustainability, but the auditor notes this depends on achieving a balanced budget in 2025/26—which the Council is not currently on track to deliver.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion to cover current-year overspend is unsustainable. The stated intention to rebuild reserves is contingent on a budget performance the Council has not yet demonstrated it can achieve, making the reserve plan unrealistic.
findings.figures: Earmarked reserves reduced by £11m: from £29.2m to £18m; plan to transfer £1m in 2025/26 contingent on balanced budget
findings.quote: Earmarked reserves reduced by £11 million (from £29.2m million to £18m million) to support the delivery of the 2024/25 budget, including meeting the cost of the Council's overspend in that year. For the 2025-26 budget, the Council has set out an intention to transfer £1 million to reserves to build financial sustainability. However, this depends on the Council's delivering a balanced budget in 2025-26, which it is not currently on track to do.

findings.headline: July 2025 cashflow forecast shows negative liquidity of (£84.04m) at 31 March 2026 without further borrowing
findings.detail: Management's July 2025 cashflow forecast shows a cash opening balance of £13.57 million on 1 April 2025 and a closing balance of (£84.04) million at 31 March 2026. The auditor notes this means the Council will need to borrow further to fund day-to-day expenditure, at additional cost. Liquidity levels are described as 'impacted significantly' by financial pressures and should be 'closely monitored'.
findings.matters: Projected negative liquidity is a critical warning sign. A council that cannot fund its day-to-day operations without emergency borrowing is in acute financial distress and poses material credit risk.
findings.figures: £13.57m cash opening balance; (£84.04m) closing balance 31 March 2026 without further borrowing
findings.quote: The July 2025 Cashflow forecast provided by management shows a cash opening balance of £13.57 million on 1 April 2025 and closing balance of (£84.04) million at 31 March 2026 without further additional debt refinancing, which means that the Council will need to borrow further to fund day to day expenditure.

findings.headline: External debt of £458.5m exceeds £445.7m target and debt servicing costs are 16% of net revenue
findings.detail: The Council holds £458.5 million in loans as of 31 March 2025, exceeding its £445.7 million target by £12.8 million due to delayed asset disposals. Debt servicing costs represent around 16% of the 2025/26 net revenue stream, which is material and constrains flexibility for new borrowing or service investment.
findings.matters: Debt above target with high servicing costs limits the Council's borrowing capacity and financial flexibility. High debt service ratios reduce headroom for managing volatility or taking on new liabilities.
findings.figures: £458.5m in loans vs £445.7m target (£12.8m overage); debt servicing 16% of 2025/26 net revenue
findings.quote: External debt pressures also persist, with the Council holding £458.5 million in loans as of 31 March 2025, exceeding its £445.7 million target, due to delayed asset disposals. Debt servicing costs are around 16% of the 2025/26 net revenue stream.

findings.headline: Asset disposal programme 54.8% below forecast, with capital receipts revised from £86.23m to £39m (2024/25–2026/27)
findings.detail: Forecasted capital receipts from asset disposals for the three-year period 2024/25–2026/27 were revised downward from £86.23 million to £39.0 million, a reduction of 54.8%. The auditor identifies the asset disposal programme as a critical risk and notes it is not on track. This directly impacts liquidity and the Council's ability to fund day-to-day expenditure.
findings.matters: Asset sales are a core pillar of the Council's financial plan; a miss of this magnitude calls into question both the realism of financial forecasting and the Council's ability to access this revenue source. It forces reliance on borrowing to maintain liquidity.
findings.figures: Capital receipts revised from £86.23m to £39.0m (54.8% reduction) for 2024/25–2026/27
findings.quote: Forecasted capital receipts from asset disposals for 2024/25–2026/27 were revised from £86.23 million to £39.0 million—a 54.8% drop.

findings.headline: Medium-term funding gap of £105.3m (2026/27–2029/30) increased by £29.5m since March 2025
findings.detail: The Council's refreshed MTFS projects a cumulative funding gap of £105.3 million for 2026/27 to 2029/30, representing a significant deterioration of £29.5 million compared to the March 2025 position. This gap remains unresolved despite commissioners' intervention since 2022.
findings.matters: A widening medium-term gap signals that the Council's transformation and savings plans are not delivering, and existing interventions are not closing the structural deficit. This is unsustainable without further external support.
findings.figures: £105.3m cumulative gap 2026/27–2029/30; increase of £29.5m since March 2025
findings.quote: The Council's refreshed Medium-Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) projects a cumulative funding gap of £105.3 million for 2026/27 to 2029/30 — an increase of £29.5 million since March 2025.

findings.headline: Budget overspent by £8.8m in 2024/25 and Q1 2025/26 forecasts emerging pressure of £13.8m despite balanced budget
findings.detail: The Council overspent its £160.2 million service budget by £8.8 million in 2024/25, funded from reserves. Despite setting a balanced budget for 2025/26 following extensive planning, Q1 forecasts emerging pressures of £13.8 million. The Dedicated Schools Grant also remains under pressure with a net overspend and high-risk trajectory for High Needs spending.
findings.matters: A council unable to deliver a balanced budget and facing growing in-year pressures signals structural budget problems and weak financial control, presenting material risk to any new borrowing.
findings.figures: £8.8m overspend on £160.2m budget; £13.8m Q1 pressure in 2025/26; DSG net overspend £0.081m
findings.quote: In 2024/25, the Council overspent its £160.2 million service budget by £8.8 million, which was funded from reserves. The Council set a balanced budget for 2025/26 following extensive planning and scrutiny, but its Q1 report forecasts emerging pressures of £13.8 million.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant is also in overspend alongside General Fund, compounding budget control problems
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG), which funds school services, is mentioned as contributing to the £18.3m additional borrowing requirement alongside General Fund overspends. DSG deficits typically reflect demand-driven pressures, particularly in special educational needs (SEND) services.
findings.matters: DSG deficits indicate structural spending problems that accumulate year-on-year and are difficult to control. They signal that the council cannot manage school-related costs within available funding, creating a forward liability.
findings.figures: DSG contributing to £18.3m additional borrowing requirement (specific DSG overspend amount not disclosed in this report)
findings.quote: The additional borrowing is due to the financial pressure on the General Fund (£17.5m overspend at Period 2) and the Dedicated Schools Grant.

findings.headline: New borrowing required at 4.76% while average portfolio rate is 3.59%, increasing debt costs
findings.detail: New refinancing loans during the first six months were taken at 4.763% (PWLB EIP loans), while the council repaid older debt at 4.731%. The weighted average rate on the portfolio is 3.59% over 9.13 years, but with £18.3m additional borrowing now forecast, the portfolio average will rise. Interest payments to September were £7.0m but will increase materially as more debt is added.
findings.matters: Borrowing at rates over 4.7% when seeking to recover from financial distress significantly increases future debt-servicing costs. Each £1m of additional borrowing costs ~£47,600 annually, adding to already-stretched revenue budgets.
findings.figures: Refinancing loans at 4.763% average; repaid debt at 4.731%; portfolio weighted average 3.59%; interest paid to Sept £7.0m
findings.quote: £30.2m of loans have been repaid at an average rate of 4.731%, and £30.0m of refinancing loans were required to ensure liquidity, a net reduction of £0.2m over the period. The refinancing loans were PWLB Equal Instalment Payment (EIP) loans at an average rate of 4.763%.

findings.headline: External debt increased £3.7m in Q2 despite no change year-to-date, driven by revenue overspends
findings.detail: External debt at 30 September was £458.3m, representing an increase of £3.7m from the Q1 position of £454.6m. The increase was driven by General Fund and DSG net overspends, only partially offset by capital and HRA underspends. This mid-year deterioration contradicts the expectation of steady debt reduction.
findings.matters: Rising mid-year external debt driven by revenue overspends—not planned capital investment—indicates the financial recovery plan is off-track. The council is accumulating debt to cover operational shortfalls, a sign of structural budget problems.
findings.figures: External debt £454.6m (Q1) to £458.3m (30 Sept), £3.7m increase
findings.quote: It is £3.7m higher than the first quarter position of £454.6m reported to Audit and Risk Committee in November 2025, as a consequence of General Fund revenue and DSG net overspends, partly mitigated by capital and HRA net underspends.

findings.headline: Council requested £14.75m in Exceptional Financial Support for 2023/24, indicating ongoing financial distress
findings.detail: The opening Capital Financing Requirement was increased by £14.75m to reflect additional Exceptional Financial Support requested for the prior year. This exceptional support is a marker of severe financial difficulty and has increased the council's total CFR from the budgeted £668.0m to £688.5m.
findings.matters: Councils requiring Exceptional Financial Support are in material financial distress. The fact that this support is now incorporated into the baseline indicates the council has not returned to financial stability and continues to rely on government intervention.
findings.figures: £14.75m additional Exceptional Financial Support; opening CFR £688.5m vs TMS estimate £668.0m
findings.quote: Following completion of the draft Statement of Accounts for 2024/25 the opening Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) for the year has been amended, taking account of the impact of the additional Exceptional Financial Support of £14.75m requested for 2023/24

findings.headline: General Fund overspend of £17.5m at mid-year is driving additional borrowing of £18.3m
findings.detail: The council reported a £17.5m General Fund overspend at Period 2, which is the primary driver of an £18.3m increase in the full-year external debt forecast from £436.7m to £455.0m. This means the council cannot absorb operational overspends from underspends elsewhere and is instead borrowing to cover them.
findings.matters: A mid-year General Fund overspend indicates spending control is not improving as the council claims to be in financial recovery. Borrowing to cover operational shortfalls rather than capital investment increases long-term debt-servicing costs and suggests the financial trajectory is deteriorating.
findings.figures: £17.5m overspend at Period 2; borrowing forecast increased from £436.7m to £455.0m (£18.3m increase)
findings.quote: The additional borrowing is due to the financial pressure on the General Fund (£17.5m overspend at Period 2) and the Dedicated Schools Grant.

findings.headline: Significant weaknesses in Children's Services and SEND with statutory directions in place
findings.detail: Due to longstanding statutory direction on Children's Services (renewed yearly) and a new statutory direction on SEND, the Authority has significant weaknesses in performance. Auditors recommended the Authority work with the Department for Education to improve performance in both areas.
findings.matters: Statutory directions indicate central government has lost confidence in the council's ability to protect vulnerable children; these services are high-cost and subject to enforcement intervention.
findings.figures: Statutory direction on Children's Services (renewed yearly); new statutory direction on SEND
findings.quote: Due to the longstanding (renewed yearly) statutory direction on Children's Services and the new SEND statutory direction on SEND, the Authority has significant weaknesses in the performance of Children's Services.

findings.headline: Transformation programme underfunded with only £4m allocated for 2021/22 and 2022/23
findings.detail: The Authority's Transformation Programme (running to 31 March 2026) allocated £4 million for 2021/22 and 2022/23, which auditors determined is insufficient for the scale of transformation needed to exit intervention. The programme lacks adequate plans to exit intervention.
findings.matters: The underfunded transformation programme lacks the resources to deliver the systemic change needed to restore financial sustainability or exit government intervention status.
findings.figures: £4 million allocated to transformation programme for 2021/22 and 2022/23
findings.quote: There was £4 million allocated to the transformation programme for 2021/22 and 2022/23 and this is insufficient for the scale of transformation the Authority needs to deliver.

findings.headline: Extreme senior management turnover with four Section 151 Officers in five years
findings.detail: Since 1 April 2021 the Authority has had four Chief Executives, four Section 151 Officers, five Monitoring Officers, two Directors of Adult Social Services and three Directors of Children's Social Care. Auditors recommended maintaining permanence of the senior leadership team.
findings.matters: This level of turnover in finance leadership (four CFO equivalents in 5 years) indicates systemic dysfunction, loss of institutional knowledge, and inability to retain senior talent.
findings.figures: 4 Chief Executives, 4 Section 151 Officers, 5 Monitoring Officers since 1 April 2021
findings.quote: Since 1 April 2021 there have been four Chief Executives, four Section 151 Officers, five Monitoring Officers, two Directors of Adult Social Services and three Directors of Children's Social Care.

findings.headline: Auditors identified inadequate internal controls and delays in preparing financial statements; accounts published 31 October 2025
findings.detail: Auditors identified significant weaknesses in governance arrangements relating to inadequate arrangements for reliable and timely financial reporting due to poor internal controls and delays in the preparation and publication of the annual statement of accounts. These weaknesses remained in 2022-23 and 2023-24.
findings.matters: Persistent delays in producing accounts (7 months late) prevent stakeholders, including creditors, from understanding the council's position on time and indicate control failures.
findings.figures: Accounts published 31 October 2025, missing 16 January 2025 deadline
findings.quote: inadequate arrangements to ensure reliable and timely financial reporting due to poor internal controls and delays in the preparation and publication of the annual statement of accounts

findings.headline: Medium-term financial plan relies heavily on asset disposal programme with uncertain, unvalidated assumptions
findings.detail: On 31 October 2024 auditors identified a further significant weakness: the Authority's Medium Term financial plan depends heavily on an asset disposal programme and funding derived from capital receipts. Assurance could not be gained that the plan is predicated on appropriate, reasonable and robust assumptions, or what consideration had been given to the Authority's future operating model.
findings.matters: A financial recovery plan based on uncertain asset sales rather than operational improvements is high-risk; if receipts fall short, the council cannot meet its obligations.
findings.figures: Asset disposal programme underpins Medium Term financial plan
findings.quote: Assurance was not able to be gained that the plan is predicated on appropriate, reasonable and robust assumptions; and what level of consideration had been undertaken for the future operating model of the Authority.

findings.headline: Council lacks adequate reserves and requires ongoing central government capitalisation directions to balance budget
findings.detail: On 22 May 2024 auditors identified that Slough did not have an adequate level of reserves, necessitating central government support through a capitalisation direction. A capitalisation direction was agreed for 2018/19 to 2022/23, and subsequently for 2023/24 to set a balanced budget. Errors in financial reporting further reduced forecast reserves.
findings.matters: Chronic reserve inadequacy and budget-dependent bailouts from central government signal the council cannot fund its operations independently and is insolvent without ongoing support.
findings.figures: Capitalisation directions 2018/19 to 2022/23, then 2023/24
findings.quote: the Authority did not have an adequate level of reserves and the requirement for central government support delivered through a capitalisation direction

findings.headline: £46.325m capitalisation direction included in accounts without MHCLG confirmation it is permitted
findings.detail: The 2023-24 financial statements include accounting entries totalling £46.325m for an MHCLG capitalisation direction, but MHCLG has not confirmed that Slough is permitted to include this sum. The auditors were unable to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence to support this balance. Had they not disclaimed their opinion, this alone would have led to a qualified opinion.
findings.matters: A material unconfirmed asset representing a significant portion of the accounts creates extreme uncertainty about the council's actual financial position; any reversal would be catastrophic.
findings.figures: £46.325m capitalisation direction
findings.quote: To date MHCLG has not confirmed that the Authority is permitted to include this sum in the financial statements and thus we were unable to obtain sufficient, appropriate evidence to support this balance. Had we not disclaimed our opinion, this matter would have led us to modify our opinion on the financial statements.

findings.headline: Journal control and accounting record issues from 2018/19 remain unresolved through 2023/24
findings.detail: The council operated without appropriate journal controls in 2018/19, with many accounting entries having limited or no supporting evidence, and entries posted outside the general ledger that were unsupported and poorly documented. The authority also did not maintain adequate accounting records to support entries in the trial balance. These two matters have not been resolved in the current year.
findings.matters: Unresolved systemic control failures over a five-year period indicate fundamental weaknesses in financial record-keeping and the risk of undetected errors throughout the accounts.
findings.figures: Issues from 2018/19 remain unresolved through 2023-24
findings.quote: Both these matters have not been resolved in the current year and because of the limitations imposed by the backstop date, we have been unable to determine whether their impact on the current year financial statements impact could be both material and pervasive.

findings.headline: Auditors disclaim opinion on the 2023-24 accounts due to insufficient audit evidence by the backstop date
findings.detail: Grant Thornton cannot express an opinion on Slough's financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2024 because they were unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence by the 28 February 2025 backstop date. The council published unaudited accounts on 31 October 2025, missing the 16 January 2025 deadline for unaudited accounts to preserve elector rights. The possible effects of undetected misstatements are considered both material and pervasive.
findings.matters: A disclaimer of opinion means the accounts cannot be relied upon and the council's true financial position is unknown; this is the most serious audit finding possible.
findings.figures: Backstop date 28 February 2025; accounts published 31 October 2025; deadline for unaudited accounts 16 January 2025
findings.quote: We have not been able to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence by the backstop date to conclude that the Authority's or group's financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2024 as a whole are free from material misstatement.

findings.headline: Bad debt provision reductions and Council Tax Support cuts substituting for service efficiency
findings.detail: Below-the-line savings include £0.883m reduction in bad debt provision plus £0.500m removal of sundry debt provision and £0.724m reduction in CTS expenditure. These are accounting adjustments and welfare cuts rather than operational or structural efficiency improvements.
findings.matters: These measures are less sustainable than service efficiency; they depend on collection performance holding and may not be replicable year-on-year or may create policy risk if welfare support reductions face challenge.

findings.headline: Adults Services savings dominated by reduction in care hours across working and older adults
findings.detail: Adults Services accounts for £2.310m of 2026/27 savings through multiple proposals to reduce home care hours via reassessment and optimisation of complex care, with ongoing reductions continuing into 2028/29 (£1.352m). Savings depend on successful care reduction and contract review of Mental Health services (ASC-2627-S05).
findings.matters: Service reductions of this scale in adult social care may impact quality or outcomes; this is a load-bearing part of the budget plan that carries risk if care demand or outcomes pressure forces reversal.

findings.headline: Most identified savings are one-year-only with no ongoing benefit to future years
findings.detail: The majority of the £12.029m package of proposals show activity only in 2026/27 with zeros across 2027/28, 2028/29, and 2029/30. This includes corporate IT equipment releases, software terminations, training reductions, and procurement savings. The council will need to identify equivalent new savings each subsequent year to maintain current budget levels.
findings.matters: One-off savings do not improve structural financial sustainability; year-on-year recurrence signals the council faces persistent underlying budget gaps.

findings.headline: Business Rate one-off gain of £4.431m (37% of annual plan) explicitly reverses in 2027/28
findings.detail: The 2026/27 savings plan includes a £4.431m one-off improvement from rateable value finder exercise that completely reverses to a cost in 2027/28. This one-off measure dominates the package and will not contribute to budget sustainability or underlying structural savings.
findings.matters: Lenders assess whether savings plans are structural or built on accounting one-offs; a plan that is over one-third one-off and reverses signals the council faces larger underlying pressures.
findings.figures: COR-2627-S19: (4.431) in 26/27, reverses to 4.431 cost in 27/28. Total 2026/27 savings: (12.029).
findings.quote: Business Rate collection improvement - one-off gain from Rateable Value finder exercise

findings.headline: External interest paid only £0.40m versus budget of £4.54m in Q1—91% underspend
findings.detail: External interest paid in Q1 totalled £0.40m against a budget of £4.54m, a variance of £4.15m. The underspend was broad-based: General Fund £3.16m under budget and HRA £0.98m under. This unusually large variance suggests planned borrowing levels are not materializing or debt levels are significantly lower than budgeted.
findings.matters: A major shortfall in expected interest payments could indicate that the council's borrowing programme is stalling, which could delay capital project delivery or signal that capital spending is being deferred from budget plans.
findings.figures: Interest paid £0.40m vs budgeted £4.54m (£4.15m underspend); General Fund £0.22m vs £3.39m; HRA £0.17m vs £1.15m
findings.quote: Total external interest paid on an accrual basis during the period was £0.40 million, which was £4.15 million below the budget.

findings.headline: No new borrowing undertaken in Q1 despite £81.16m annual capital expenditure forecast
findings.detail: The council did not undertake new borrowing in Q1 2025/26 for capital expenditure, despite forecasting £81.16m spending for the year. Instead, £10m of PWLB loans were refinanced and £13.91m was repaid. With the elevated CFR forecast, this suggests capital is being funded from reserves or capital receipts rather than new borrowing.
findings.matters: Funding capital from reserves rather than borrowing could lead to reserve depletion and reduce the council's financial buffers to manage unexpected pressures or funding shortfalls.
findings.figures: No new capital borrowing in Q1; £81.16m capital expenditure forecast 2025/26; £5.822m capital receipts achieved Q1
findings.quote: No new borrowing was undertaken for capital expenditure during the period.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement forecast £72m above budget at £718.76m
findings.detail: The 2025/26 year-end CFR forecast is £718.76m versus the budgeted assumption of £646.70m approved in March. The opening CFR was also materially higher at £721.20m against £668.0m assumed. This represents substantial capital spending above original plans, with implications for long-term debt levels.
findings.matters: Higher capital financing requirements drive higher debt levels and long-term servicing costs, which affects the affordability of the council's debt and its financial sustainability.
findings.figures: 2025/26 forecast CFR £718.76m vs budgeted £646.70m (£72.06m variance); Opening CFR £721.20m vs assumed £668.0m
findings.quote: For 2025/26, the CFR assumed at the year-end in the Treasury Management Strategy was £646.70 million. However, the latest forecast suggests the closing CFR will be £718.76 million, reflecting updated opening position and current capital expenditure expectations.

findings.headline: £14.75m Exceptional Financial Support application from MHCLG remains subject to approval
findings.detail: The council's opening Capital Financing Requirement includes a pending £14.75m application to MHCLG for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) from 2023/24 in the form of a capitalisation direction. This application is subject to approval, indicating the council required government financial support in the prior year.
findings.matters: Government bailout funding signals prior year financial distress. A lender must track whether approval is granted, as it directly affects the council's financial position and ability to manage future borrowing.
findings.figures: £14.75m EFS 2023/24 capitalisation direction pending
findings.quote: the application to MHCLG for £14.75m of additional Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) 2023/24, in the form of capitalisation direction, is reflected in the revised opening CFR. The additional EFS is subject to approval.

findings.headline: Council faces material interest rate risk on £454.57m debt; interest costs already running below budget by £4.15m
findings.detail: The Council carries £454.57m in external borrowing at current 3.57% average rate, with interest paid £4.15m below budget in Q1. Risk management identifies that interest rate rises are a key threat. Each 0.5% rise would add approximately £2.27m to annual debt service costs, materially impacting the recovery plan.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the Council's financial stability must factor that recent interest savings mask underlying exposure; debt service costs rise significantly if rates increase from current levels
findings.figures: £454.57m borrowing, 3.57% average rate, £4.15m Q1 interest saving vs budget
findings.quote: During the period external borrowing decreased from £458.48 to £454.57 million at an average rate of 3.57%, with no new borrowing undertaken for capital purposes. Investment balances ranged from £10.04 million to £47.26 million, with a closing balance of £23.55 million and a return of 4.33%. Investment income was marginally below budget by £0.01 million, while external interest paid was £4.15 million below budget.

findings.headline: Council is explicitly in financial recovery mode and has identified asset sale delays as a material risk to recovery plan
findings.detail: The Council acknowledges it is 'on a journey to get back onto a financially sustainable footing' through debt reduction and asset disposals. Risk management section flags that asset sales may not generate expected receipts or be delayed, with direct impact on 'financing the capitalisation directions', indicating recovery hinges on execution of this strategy.
findings.matters: Explicit statement of financial recovery mode combined with identified execution risk (asset sale delays) signals the council is managing tight financial constraints and recovery depends on successful completion of its disposal programme
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: The Council is on a journey to get back onto a financially sustainable footing, a key element of which is by reducing debt, and by disposing of assets.

findings.headline: Financial recovery strategy depends heavily on asset disposals: £5.822m generated in Q1 alone
findings.detail: The Council generated £5.822m in capital receipts from asset disposals in Q1 (£2.425m from General Fund, £3.397m from HRA). The Council explicitly states its recovery programme relies on asset disposals as a key mechanism to reduce debt. This strategy is vulnerable if property market conditions deteriorate or sale timings slip.
findings.matters: A lender must assess whether debt reduction is sustainable; heavy dependence on property sales creates refinancing risk if the market weakens or sales stall
findings.figures: £5.822m Q1 capital receipts (£2.425m General Fund, £3.397m HRA)
findings.quote: During Q1 2025/26, the Council generated £5.822 million in capital receipts from asset disposals, £2.425 million from the General Fund (including 4 disposals to the HRA) and £3.397 million from the HRA.

findings.headline: External debt declined modestly in Q1 but the Council remains a long-term borrower with no new capital borrowing
findings.detail: External borrowing fell from £458.48m to £454.57m at an average rate of 3.57%. The Council undertook no new borrowing for capital purposes during the quarter. This modest £3.91m reduction, combined with the Council's reliance on asset disposals, suggests capital investment capacity is severely constrained.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the council's debt trajectory needs to see whether debt reduction is structural or asset-sale-driven; the lack of new capital borrowing signals either strong capital discipline or restricted borrowing capacity
findings.figures: £458.48m opening, £454.57m closing, 3.57% average rate
findings.quote: During the period external borrowing decreased from £458.48 to £454.57 million at an average rate of 3.57%, with no new borrowing undertaken for capital purposes.

findings.headline: Council received £14.75m exceptional financial support as capitalisation direction to address prior financial distress
findings.detail: The Council's opening Capital Financing Requirement for 2025/26 was amended to include a request for £14.75m Exceptional Financial Support in the form of a capitalisation direction, as reflected in the 2023/24 draft Statement of Accounts. Capitalisation direction converts debt into non-debt funding, indicating government intervention to address a financing shortfall.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council required government bail-out support, confirming prior financial stress and ongoing recovery dependence
findings.figures: £14.75m capitalisation direction
findings.quote: The opening 2025/26 Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) has now been amended to reflect finalisation of backlog accounts to 2023/24, plus the request for an additional £14.75m Exceptional Financial Support in the form of capitalisation direction, as reflected in the 2023/24 draft Statement of Accounts.

findings.paper_title: Rec of Audit - TM Outturn 2425 Appendix - Final
findings.headline: Slough Children First £5m loan fully repaid, reducing non-treasury investment portfolio
findings.detail: The £5m loan to Slough Children First that was outstanding at 31 March 2024 was fully repaid on 31 March 2025 with £0.08m interest. Combined with other movements, total interest receivable from non-treasury investments fell from £2.12m to £1.86m year-on-year. The repayment signals a change in the council's relationship with this entity.
findings.matters: A finance director must understand whether this company (which provides children's services) is now self-financing, whether the council has exited the investment, or whether alternative arrangements exist; it also reduces the council's investment income
findings.figures: £5m loan repaid; interest payment £0.08m; total non-treasury investment income fell from £2.12m to £1.86m
findings.quote: The £5m of Slough Children First loan was repaid on 31st March 2025 together with payment of £0.08m of interest.

findings.paper_title: Rec of Audit - TM Outturn 2425 Appendix - Final
findings.headline: Capital expenditure underspent by £10.85m (22%) on General Fund, £1.40m (7%) on HRA
findings.detail: General Fund capital expenditure came in at £37.57m against a budget of £48.42m; HRA capital at £18.24m against £19.64m. The report notes that delayed asset disposal sales and end-of-year payment timing affected the borrowing position. This level of underspend suggests planned capital projects did not progress as scheduled.
findings.matters: A lender tracks whether councils deliver their capital programmes; a 22% underspend raises questions about project delays, delivery capacity, or reduced capital ambition, all of which affect the council's financial flexibility and economic contribution
findings.figures: General Fund: £48.42m budget, £37.57m actual (£10.85m underspend, 22%); HRA: £19.64m budget, £18.24m actual (£1.40m underspend, 7%)

findings.paper_title: Rec of Audit - TM Outturn 2425 Appendix - Final
findings.headline: Cabinet increased GRE 5 lending commitment from £10m to £15m pending receipt of Homes England grant
findings.detail: The council extended its loan facility to GRE 5 Ltd from £10m to £15m. The reported reason for the increase was to enable works to be completed, pending finalisation of a grant from Homes England. The actual loan balance at 31 March 2025 was £5.17m. If grant funding is delayed or reduced, the council may face pressure to fund the additional £5m facility itself.
findings.matters: A capital lending facility contingent on an external grant carries both execution and grant realization risk; if Homes England grant is withheld or delayed, the council's capital plans or borrowing may be affected
findings.figures: Facility increased from £10m to £15m; actual balance £5.17m at 31/3/2025; grant pending from Homes England
findings.quote: Cabinet approved the extension of the GRE 5 loan facility agreement up to £15m (from £10m) at its meeting of April 2023. The increased in loan required pending finalisation of the grant to be received from Homes England and to enable works to be completed.

findings.paper_title: Rec of Audit - TM Outturn 2425 Appendix - Final
findings.headline: Council fell below its voluntary £10m liquidity threshold on 9 separate occasions in Q1 2024/25
findings.detail: In the first quarter of 2024/25, the council's cash balance dropped below its voluntary £10m liquidity threshold nine times. Each breach was resolved within 24 hours, but the frequency indicates working capital stress. This did not recur in the remaining three quarters. The council's strategy of using internal cash balances to fund capital rather than external borrowing may be contributing to tighter liquidity.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether this Q1 pattern reflects structural cash flow tightness or a one-off timing issue; repeated near-breaches of liquidity thresholds indicate dependence on predictable inflows and vulnerability to collection delays
findings.figures: 9 separate occasions in first quarter only; voluntary threshold £10m; replenished within 24 hours in each case
findings.quote: on 9 separate occasions during the first quarter of 2024/25 the Council fell below its voluntary liquidity threshold of £10m. In each case, the cash balance was replenished within 24 hours. It was not breached during the rest of the financial year.

findings.paper_title: IA progress Report - Appx B Compliance with Prudential Code
findings.headline: Audit finds governance framework effective; non-compliance limited to indicator disclosure and quarterly report timing
findings.detail: The audit concludes that the council's governance arrangements for treasury management and capital finance are working effectively. Full Council, Cabinet, and Committee responsibilities are being met. The Capital Strategy framework is in place and integrated with revenue and capital planning. The auditors found no key risks and recommend no health check review for 2025-26. Compliance gaps are confined to specific indicator disclosures and timeliness of quarterly reporting.
findings.matters: Provides assurance that decision-making and oversight structures are functioning; the compliance gaps appear to be administrative or timing issues rather than structural control failures
findings.figures: No key risks identified
findings.quote: On balance, the findings demonstrate an effective governance framework is in place and no key risks have been identified which would support the conclusion that a health check review be undertaken as part of the 2025/26 internal audit plan.

findings.paper_title: IA progress Report - Appx B Compliance with Prudential Code
findings.headline: Financing costs to net revenue stream indicator disclosed for only two years instead of required three-year period
findings.detail: The prudential indicator on financing costs as a proportion of net revenue stream has been disclosed only for years 1 and 2 of the medium-term planning period. Year 3 (2027-28) budget figures are absent from quarterly reports, the mid-year review, and the draft treasury strategy. The council committed to extending this to a full three-year disclosure in the next Treasury Management Strategy Statement by February 2026.
findings.matters: Reduces medium-term visibility of the council's debt affordability; lenders and peer councils require full-period forecasts to assess the sustainability of financing plans
findings.figures: 2 years disclosed; year 3 (2027-28) figure missing
findings.quote: Estimates of financing costs to net revenue stream has been disclosed partially in accordance with the reporting requirements of the Prudential Code as budgeted figures for year 3 (2027-28) has not been disclosed.

findings.paper_title: IA progress Report - Appx B Compliance with Prudential Code
findings.headline: Four Prudential Code indicators have not been disclosed in compliance reporting
findings.detail: The council has not disclosed: actual capital expenditure; actual financing costs as a proportion of net revenue stream; estimates of net income from commercial and service investments as a proportion of net revenue stream; and actual net income from commercial and service investments as a proportion of net revenue stream. These indicators are required under the Prudential Code and should appear in treasury outturn reports and quarterly monitoring. The council has committed to including all four from July 2025 onwards.
findings.matters: Non-compliance with Prudential Code disclosure requirements limits transparency of the council's financial position and effectiveness of its monitoring framework
findings.figures: 4 indicators identified as non-compliant
findings.quote: Prudential Code Indicators have not been disclosed in respect of the following indicators: actual capital expenditure; actual financing costs ÷ actual net revenue stream x 100%; estimates of net income from commercial and service investments ÷ estimate of net revenue stream x 100%; and actual net income from commercial and service investments ÷ actual net revenue stream x 100%.

findings.paper_title: IA progress Report - Appx B Compliance with Prudential Code
findings.headline: Q1 2024-25 Treasury Management Report submitted three months late to committee; Q3 report also delayed
findings.detail: The quarterly Treasury Management Report for quarter 1 (ending 30 June 2024) was not submitted to the Audit and Corporate Governance Committee until 30 September 2024. The council attributed the delay to resource pressures from statutory accounts completion. The Q3 2024-25 report was similarly affected, with the scheduled March 2025 committee meeting cancelled and submission now expected in April 2025.
findings.matters: Indicates capacity constraints in the finance function and shows quarterly prudential monitoring deadlines are not being reliably met; peer finance directors should assess their own quarterly reporting resilience
findings.figures: Q1 report 3 months late; Q3 report delayed from March to April 2025
findings.quote: The Q1 2024-25 Treasury Management Report was submitted to the Committee on 30 September 2024 and audit understand the report could not have been submitted earlier due to resources directed towards completion of annual statutory accounts.

findings.detail: The Audit and Corporate Governance Committee received and noted the Outturn Report on 10 July 2024 but did not refer it onwards to Full Council, breaching Treasury Management Practice requirements. The council has agreed to implement a process to ensure future outturn reports reach Full Council, with a target date of September 2025.
findings.matters: Shows a governance process failure in oversight of treasury management reporting; peer authorities should verify their own outturn reporting escalation procedures

findings.quote: The Audit and Corporate Governance Committee received a copy of the Treasury Management Outturn Report 2023-24 at the 10 July 2024 meeting where after due consideration the report was noted, however, the report was not referred to the Full Council.

news_drafts.headline: Slough forecasts £417.4m of exceptional financial support, £336.4m of it formally agreed to 2024/25
news_drafts.lead:
Slough Council's medium term financial strategy (MTFS) forecasts exceptional financial support totalling £417.4m, according to the draft budget update report for its Cabinet meeting on 16 November. Exceptional financial support is permission from government to borrow, or sell assets, to cover day-to-day spending. The paper says: "The agreed level of EFS as forecast in the MTFS totals £417.4m".

Of that total, £336.4m was formally agreed up to 2024/25. The remainder is set out year by year in the paper's table: £15.7m for 2025/26, £42.9m for 2026/27 and an indicative £22.4m for 2027/28.

The paper says the amounts for 2025/26, 2026/27 and the indicative 2027/28 are agreed in principle or indicative. It says they will be formally agreed only once the council's accounts have been audited and signed off.

news_drafts.headline: Slough's 2025/26 overspend came in at £13.2m against a forecast £20.7m; 2026/27 budget not yet balanced
news_drafts.lead:
Slough Borough Council ended 2025/26 with an overspend of £13.2m, after applying £15.7m of exceptional financial support (EFS), permission from government to borrow or sell assets to cover day-to-day spending. The council had forecast an overspend of £20.7m. Its external auditor's interim annual audit report says the forecast overspend "was contained" to £13.2m by year end.

The auditor attributes the reduction to measures introduced during the year, including freezing non-essential recruitment and reducing agency and interim staff. The overspend was predominantly in temporary accommodation and housing benefit subsidy loss, which together came to £13.8m.

For 2026/27, the auditor reports the council "has been unable to set a balanced budget" without additional EFS, with £42.9m approved in principle. The medium-term plan anticipated a further £22.4m in 2027/28. The council's Annual Governance Statement update for the second quarter rates red its inability to produce a draft budget for November that balances within its existing EFS assumptions. A detailed report on the budget and medium-term financial strategy is due at Cabinet in November 2026. The government's commissioners at the council describe financial sustainability as their "prime concern". The council's s.151 officer, its chief finance officer, said in a report to Full Council that it is not financially sustainable without EFS.

news_drafts.headline: Slough faces material risk to reserves as services miss financial targets
news_drafts.lead: Slough's audit committee heard that the council faces a material risk of needing to draw on its reserves during the current financial year in ways it did not plan for, and that this could trigger urgent debt refinancing. The risk reflects deeper problems: housing is not meeting the financial assumptions in the medium-term financial strategy (the council's three-to-five-year spending plan), the capital programme is slipping without clear explanation, and the children's services company needs external review before further funding is committed. The auditors have also found that debtor and creditor records lack clean transaction data, making it difficult to verify year-end balances and completing a full in-year audit unlikely. The council's governance assessment rated financial management red on reserves and treasury arrangements, and amber on savings delivery and growth mitigation. Value for money findings are due in November.
